Combined with the Remaining Examples and Discursive Treatises on the Doctrines of the Exoteric Teachings, Part Two:
A Treatise on the Ten Categories of Adoption and Abolition in the Tiantai School (End).
In the first fascicle of the *Tiantai School’s Treatise on the Ten Categories of Adoption and Rejection*, it is stated:

"Because one enters [the path] only after investigation and examination, the two kinds of emptiness (*dvaya-śūnyatā*) follow next. These two emptinesses are also contemplations of phenomena (*dharmas*);

they are merely the application of medicine according to the illness. Therefore, it is said: 'During the Buddha's lifetime, these were suited to the specific capacities of the audience; why labor to establish them? Although they may be appropriate for the period after his parinirvāṇa..."

Furthermore, because this also extends to the Buddha-world, there is the illusion of the four natures' non-arising according to the Shared Teaching. Now, the non-arising of the four natures is precisely emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Because it is precisely emptiness, it contains the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*). Containing the Middle Way serves as the basis for being "received" [into the distinct teaching].
Therefore, it is followed by the stage of being received. However, being received is that which belongs to the path of the teachings; thus, it is said that the preceding six stages still...
The path of teaching is preserved prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. It accommodates those of provisional capacity, for the provisional capacity is suited to the path of teaching.

The path of teaching must ultimately lead to the path of realization; therefore, it is followed by the teaching-realization. Teaching-realization refers to the movement from the provisional toward the real.
When one reaches ultimate reality, the path of teaching may be relinquished; there remains only the single, perfect reality, which is the beginning of the true cause.

Since a cause must necessarily have a fruit, this is followed by the "Life Span" (āyus-pramāṇa). The Life Span concerns the matter of the person who has attained the fruit, yet it must depend upon a body.

Since a body must necessarily have a land, this is followed by the "Four Lands. This is because the three bodies (trikāya) necessarily depend upon the four lands. Thus, the Four Lands [are explained].
The ultimate limit of this [teaching] is rooted in the *jigguang* (tranquil light). This *jigguang* rational nature (*xing*) returns to the essence of the sūtra’s body.

Thus, although the ten categories differ, they circulate and revolve, arising through both retrograde and progressive sequences; they serve as one another’s beginning and end within a single path. What is this single path?
It is precisely the ultimately pure path that transcends birth and death. Wherein does this path reside?
This is precisely the mind itself. Thus, one sees that all phenomena do not depart from one’s own mind.
Those who study this text should strive to approximate this realization; otherwise, to waste days and labor upon it without such attainment—I have never seen how that could be possible.
How profound is this exposition! How can one fail to know this beforehand and reflect upon it with careful scrutiny?
The Treatise on the Essence of the Sūtras, Part One (Each Section Divided into Three).
General Preface, Upper Section.
The Treatise states: Now, that single word which exhausts the root of all dharmas, and that single principle which reaches the ultimate source of all wonders—this can be none other than...
This is the essence of the sūtra. Therefore, the discourse on the essence of the sūtra is truly not easy to express.
Thus, those who speak of it must be ones who have severed the path of the mind and extinguished discursive thought, being able to do so by means of "speech that is no speech.

For its essence takes the nature of all phenomena and is not something obtained through artificial construction; when expressed in a sūtra, it cannot be reached through names or words. Having no choice, one is compelled to [speak of it] by force.
To discern this, there is only the Middle Way, the Seal of the Single True Reality (*eka-tattva-lakṣaṇa-mudrā*). By means of this single seal, all teachings are authenticated;
it is something that neither Māras nor non-Buddhists can share. If they cannot even share it, how much less could they differ from or destroy it?
Therefore, the Sūtras have an essence, just as a person has a heart, a people has a ruler, official documents have seals, and governance has rites.
The Dharma is the Eastern Sea for the hundred rivers; it is truly the Northern Dipper among the myriad stars. To revere it and to take it as the ultimate—there is but one.
Therefore, it is said that the "essence" (ti) is the final destination of a single section [of scripture] and the great confluence of all meanings.

It is further said that the "real mark of the dharma-realm" (dharmadhātu-satyalakṣaṇa), up to the "dharma-body" (dharmakāya), are all alternative names for the "nature of phenomena" (dharmatā). These collectively serve as the essence for all sutras. This is why the sutra attains...

This is the essence; therefore, it is called "possessing reality. To say that there is a purposeful intent is because the teaching attains this essence; thus, understanding reaches its destination and practice finds its refuge.
Both ordinary beings and sages follow it together, and all phenomena converge toward it. Ultimately returning to the source, it is likewise one and the same.
Yet while the discourse on principle remains broad, the essence is but a single nature. This nature is not a mere nature; nature must necessarily possess virtue.
Furthermore, the Sarvāstivāda school establishes that phenomena exist; their manifestation constitutes "names" (*nāma*), and their discernment constitutes "teachings" (*śāsana*).

Therefore, a single word regarding the essence (*tattva*) must necessarily relate to the five chapters and three categories (*tridharma*) to elucidate it. Although the ultimate realization of this principle resides in the Buddha, it does not reside exclusively in him;
thus, it is further discussed in terms of the phenomena of the ten realms (*daśadhātu*). Within this, there are the categories of the cultivated (*bhāvanā*) and the inherent nature (*prakṛti*).

There are instances of divergence and convergence; there are meanings concerning the opening and closing of the tradition, as well as the adoption of its essence, and there are textual passages in various sutras that point in different directions, none of which can be unified.
This is why exponents differ. Because they differ, the Way of the ultimate goal (*zongji*) does not become manifest.

It is for this reason that this treatise is composed. Now, what is the position of this treatise? It must be said that it takes the teachings of the Tiantai, Jingxi, and Siming traditions as the single school.

The doctrine of the orthodox transmission accords with the principles of reason and is what is naturally so; it is used to refute those heterodox views so that they may ultimately return to the ultimate correctness.
This is also the general substance of the ten categories today.
In the separate examples above, the categories and texts of the sūtra’s essence total thirty-five (wherein the commentary text below is combined into one; the same applies to subsequent examples).

Regarding the twelve instances where the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* opens [the provisional] and discards [it] to take up the essence while also producing further meanings: these concern the discernment of the essence through the separation and combination of the present and the past.

Ten. Regarding the five chapters on the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* cited from the side [of other texts], there are five. Regarding the eight instances where various sūtras take up the essential substance (*tattva*), there are four general categories.
The category of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* opening [the provisional] and abandoning [the real] to take up the essential substance (1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15).
The Treatise says: The substance of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) pervades all dharmas; it is free from all marks, neither abiding nor not abiding, having never begun [to exist].
Regarding the difference between "opening" (kai) and "abandoning" (fei), what further grounds for acceptance or rejection could there be?

Nevertheless, the discourse on opening and abandoning is rooted in the essential purport of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and its principles of provisional and ultimate meaning; this is why their modes of acceptance and rejection differ. Now, I shall discuss this in three parts. The first is:
explaining the training by borrowing from the meaning. For while the substance of the sūtra’s words is one, the phrasing sometimes explains the substance through ritual propriety (*li*), or...

Regarding the interpretation of the *Tǐ* (Body) as explaining the *Lǐ* (Ritual), the predecessors have explained it thus: they maintain that the doctrinal purports of the present and the past are distinct and not identical;

these two interpretations should be clearly distinguished and must not be conflated into one. Ziming, however, says: "The two are mutually explanatory; there is no need to seek difference between them.

Regarding the past, one simply adopts the meaning of the ritual's distinction between the honorable and the humble, which honors the principles of sovereign and father. Some, however, claim there are points of agreement and divergence.

Although the explanations of the terms are the same, their application in meaning differs. I now maintain that the theory of mutual explanation is correct, whereas the theory of distinct explanation is not.
Even when discussing similarities and differences, they are not unilaterally identical in ritual form while identical in essence;

for instance, since the rites distinguish between the roles of ruler and subject through regulated moderation, is it not the case that the rites differ even with respect to the essence? This is because there is the principle of a substantial reality upon which they depend—is this not so?
The essence is also identical to that which it relies upon. If the essence is identical, then it is one with that which equally conforms to ritual (*li*).
If ritual distinguishes between the honorable and the humble, then it is equal in essence to the noble and the lowly. Their fundamental intent is the same; who would say there is any difference?

Nevertheless, when speaking according to the intent of the various schools (*bu*), it does not preclude taking the meaning of the two identities to explain the present, while employing the meaning of the two differences to expound the past. Thus, the explanation of the intent of the schools encompasses both.
I have understood it. The theory of "opening and abandoning" (*kai-fei*) is more plausible. The second point concerns "opening and abandoning" as the grasping of the essence (*ti*).
Previously, some relied on passages stating that all phenomena do not transcend *dharmatā*; now, however, they take what the Buddha perceived as the true essence of the *dharmatā*.
Regarding those who claim this contradicts the doctrine of "opening and abandoning," they say: "If two meanings cannot coexist, why would one accept both textual passages? If the text...
Both [the provisional and the real] coexist. Why, then, do you point exclusively to one? I say: each corresponds to its own meaning; fundamentally, they do not contradict one another.
Therefore, to take both together is precisely what the intent of the respective sections dictates. To point exclusively to one is merely according to the specific textual context. Why is this so?

It is because the provisional and real dharmas of the ten realms are one and the same. Nevertheless, there are instances where one speaks from the perspective of the actual substance of the dharma, such as when it is said that although the provisional and the real differ...

Since the principle of the ten realms is identical, all may serve as its essence (*tattva*). Although there is no need to differentiate or exclude them, they are indeed the wondrous existence (*miao-you*) capable of such differentiation.
When this essence is spoken of in relation to the Buddha’s ultimate wisdom, it is both universal and specific; this is as Siming described:
"While the essence of *dharmatā* is universal across all things, its meaning as the sphere where the Tathāgata dwells is specific to the realization of the fruit. And...

This explanation remains consistent. Even in the case of the ancient schools (nikāyas), one may speak of it in this way. There are those who correctly distinguish between the provisional and the real based on the eyes and the wisdoms;

for instance, when the four eyes and two wisdoms take objects such as "difference" and so forth—which are the dharmas of the nine realms—they belong to the partial and provisional, and thus do not constitute the essence of the present sutra.
This is the meaning of "abolishing the provisional. However, if one considers that very "difference" within its own locus, there is nothing that is not the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
To say that the provisional (the finger) is identical to the real (the moon), such that both may serve as the essence, is the meaning of "opening up" the provisional.

However, without relying on the opening up of the provisional, one cannot perceive the wondrous essence that universally penetrates all things. Without relying on the setting aside of the provisional, one cannot manifest this principle, which is wondrously ultimate within all phenomena.

Therefore, I clarify this comprehensively to further demonstrate that the essence of the *Lotus Sūtra* transcends all other sūtras. This not only clarifies the doctrinal intent of the specific section, but also reveals that its textual meaning does not differ [from the ultimate truth].
As in the two passages cited above, although they do not constitute the primary intent of opening and abolishing, speaking of them generally, they are not mutually contradictory.
Thus, everything is nothing other than the Dharma-nature; is this not the very essence pervading all things? Now, taking this...
What the Buddha perceives—is this not the ultimate subtlety of all dharmas? Now, that which is the ultimate subtlety of all dharmas is what is called "limiting the extreme.
That the essence pervades all things is what is called "universal abundance. Universal abundance reverses limitation; when the extreme is limited, all becomes pervasive.
Although two meanings are thus manifested, they together reveal a single intent. It is only because from of old these were separated into two that [this distinction arose]. Therefore...
Neither "opening" nor "abandoning" applies. Third, as for whether it is subject to "being grafted onto," the essence of this present sutra is certainly not the Middle Way that is grafted upon;
however, because one must harmonize with the single vehicle to expound the intent of this section, it may also be treated as such for the purpose of discussion and selection.

There is, however, a distinction between what is accepted and what is rejected. For instance, when one adopts the "Perfect" (yuan) to connect with the "Middle Way," it may be taken as the present essence (*tǐ*);

yet, if the "but Middle" (dàn zhōng) is not [the Perfect], this is because the meaning of "partial" versus "perfect" follows the principle according to the teaching. Alternatively, if one does not distinguish the Perfect, both may be taken as the essence, because the principle of taking the Middle Way is the same;
this is because the meaning follows the principle according to the teaching. Or, both may be non-essence, because they both still carry a trace of the "square" (fang).

This is because the teaching follows the meaning of the school (*nikāya*). Alternatively, one may let the school follow the teaching, as in the aforementioned principles of "partial" (*pian*) and "complete" (*yuan*).

Thus, the selection of what is superior or inferior differs accordingly. If one suppresses the Complete Teaching (*yuan*) to connect it with the Separate Teaching (*bie*), then that which enters [the path] is correct, while that which is entered is not.

This merely excludes the object of entry, yet the subject that enters remains entirely wondrous. However, if one connects the Separate Teaching to the Shared Teaching (*tong*), then both the subject and the object are incorrect; therefore—

This excludes both [the provisional and the partial]. Therefore, the *Shu-ji* (Commentary) states: "The essence of this present sutra consists merely of the Middle that is identical with the Empty and the Provisional;

it takes up the Perfect and connects to the Partial. This refers specifically to the subject—the capacity for entry. It still excludes the Provisional and the Empty as being identical with the Middle, and excludes the Separate [Vehicle] connecting to the Perfect;

thus, both the subject and the object are negated. Some may say: "This passage contradicts the meaning of 'separating and uniting' found below, as the way it grasps the essence is the reverse. This is because they have not understood the present [context].

This is because of the meaning of the text. This shall be further clarified later. Thus, although the passage that sequentially examines the subtle and selects the essence—taking such things as the fivefold Middle Way—seems to take them all in common, its intended meaning is not so.
This is because those various objects and their dharmic characteristics are mutually related;

one proceeds from the broad toward the narrow, entering step by step until reaching the single truth among all truths, where one selects the single truth of the Middle Way, and only then is the selection complete.

Therefore, the commentary on the divination slips states: "Now, by correlating the provisional and the real to precisely demonstrate their essence and characteristics, one knows that this is done in order to clarify [the truth] by means of setting aside the provisional.
Although there are various differences, the underlying meaning does not go beyond this."
Section on Distinguishing the Essential Nature through the Method of Separation and Integration (Sections 4, 5, 8, 16, 17, 29, 31, 32, 33, 35).
The Treatise states: The ultimate of the single nature does not involve any branching or divergence. It is the primary principle of all dharmas, encompassing all meanings.

Now, because it does not involve any branching or divergence, it may indeed be said that the categories of separation and integration do not apply. Some, relying on this, do not discuss separation and integration at all. They...

This merely highlights one particular intention; it does not realize that [the essence] universally encompasses all meanings. Once the single nature is harmonized, there is nothing to which it cannot apply.

While it is appropriate to clarify the integration and separation of the sūtra’s substance, the present treatise also has three parts. The first is titled "The Source and Flow of the Textual Intent," as seen in the two commentaries on the *Guan wuliangshou jing*.
It begins by explaining the substance (*ti*) in terms of the three dharmas, and proceeds to the school’s tenet (*zong*) and function (*yong*). Now...
Each of the two commentaries offers an interpretation that appears to treat them as a single dharma; some may therefore harbor doubts regarding this.

Now, by synthesizing those various texts, it becomes clear that they do not deviate from the principle of mutual completion between the superior and inferior aspects, where each side illuminates the other, and their meaning ultimately converges upon a single path. Only through their separation and conjunction can they be fully realized.

Thus, when the two commentaries explain the essence (*tattva*) by means of the three dharmas, they are merely separating the meanings for the sake of exposition; in order to reveal the fundamental tenet, the conjunction of identity and difference is restored.
Taking one aspect each for the "Principle" (zong) and the "Function" (yong) to manifest that the three aspects of the "Essence" (ti) are both unified and distinct;

this is why they are called "mutually constituting one another from above and below. However, this merely emphasizes a partial manifestation and has not yet revealed the principle of mutual interpenetration.

Therefore, in the *Mysterious Text on the Nirvana Sutra*, the terms "Principle-Root" (zongben) and so forth were established, while the designation "Essence-Ritual" (tili) was omitted. The intent therein is to perfectly manifest that both distinction and unity are simultaneously present. This is why, now...
This is called the mutual elucidation of "this" and "that. It is because that profound text (*xuánwén*) also possesses further implications. (And so forth.

As for the *Fahua xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra), it provides a direct explanation according to the names [of the teachings], such that they appear to be each a single dharma; yet, when analyzed according to their meaning, each is also opened up into three.

The *Śāstra-śīkā* (Commentary on the Treatise) cites the *Śāstra* to establish the meaning of the unity and diversity of the essence (*tattva*) within the aggregates (*skandha*). Furthermore, it explains the essence by means of three metaphors, and the *Jì* (Record/Commentary) further divides each of these into three;
all of these constitute its essential purport. Thus, the *Xuánwén* (Profound Text) states: "To correctly manifest the essence is to directly discern the true nature (*tathatā*), etc.

This being so, there is nothing that does not serve to establish the meaning of unity and diversity. The second [point] says: "The great essence of the dharma-characteristics (*dharmalakṣaṇa*). Now...
The essence (*tǐ*) is the nature (*xìng*). Nature must necessarily have cultivation (*xiū*). The essence is the substance (*tǐ*). Substance must necessarily have function (*yòng*).
Thus, nature and essence are one; cultivation and function are each two. When one dharma is raised, two dharmas follow it. This is the principle of separation and union.
It is contained within this. Now, when clarifying the essence of the scriptures, does this consist of emphasizing separation or emphasis on integration?

Regarding their *dharmalakṣaṇa* (phenomenal characteristics), how should one discern and select between them? I reply: One must not selectively emphasize either the meaning of separation or integration.
The principle has no divergent tracks; it is simply this. Why is this so? As indicated in the preceding passage concerning separation and integration, it says: "Emptiness, the Provisional..."
Regarding the phrase "in the midst of," although it carries the meaning of "separation," "integration" is contained within it. Yet, the Four Clarifications (Sishiming) states:
"It is precisely because the Perfect (yuan) meaning is explained in isolation that this discourse on fusion cannot be established; only then is the wondrous essence revealed.

Thus, we know that regarding the body of the sutra and its separation or integration, the orthodox tradition of our school must not be understood through one-sided interpretation. Now, I shall judge this by way of my own understanding: "Separation" reveals the pervasiveness of the essence.
This collectively reveals the ultimate nature; it is wondrously in accord with the state beyond thought, and herein lies the culmination. Why is this so? As the text itself states:
"If one were to say merely that 'this' is the essence of the sutra and so forth, would this not manifest the pervasiveness of the essence?

Furthermore, it says: "If one does not individually discern each of the three, would this not reveal the ultimate nature? Coming to the concluding demonstration, it says: "Conceptual thought is extinguished and purified. Moreover—
It is said: "When the path of the mind is cut off, is this not the wondrous resonance that transcends thought? Although this is clearly stated in the texts, those who understand it are few;

because its definitive explanation is so rare, [the meaning] remains increasingly obscure. However, this refers only to the general principle. As for the dense interweaving of the textual expressions, there are passages that are not easily unraveled.
Therefore, I shall further provide an explanation, saying: "The 'separation' must be discussed individually, while the 'conjunction' should be treated in pairs."

Discrimination: The aspects of separation and union are mutually identical; their essential meaning cannot be divided. Why is this? It is because "separation" fundamentally clarifies the principle that emptiness and the provisional are identical to the substance, thereby manifesting the pervasiveness of that substance;

therefore, it is incorrect to treat them as distinct categories for the sake of comparative analysis. "Union" clarifies that practice and nature do not overlap, manifesting the ultimate principle of the perfection of nature;
therefore, it is incorrect to treat them as distinct categories for the sake of comparative analysis. As for why they are mutually identical, it is also...

This is because such is the principle of its textual structure. For instance, when it is said that the three truths are none other than the essence of the sutra, this refers to their identity within difference.

Because they are identical within difference, one simply speaks of the "three truths. Because they are discussed in terms of their differentiation, it is said that "there is nothing that is not the essence of the sutra," for all of them fully possess the Middle Way.
It is further said: "If one does not distinguish emptiness and the provisional within each of the three [natures], then they are separated while being united.
Because they are both united and separated, there are nine [aspects] within each of the three. Due to their union through discourse, one distinguishes the two [extremes] to grasp the middle.

Thus, it should be known that wherever there is a distinction, although there are nine phenomena, their meaning is already unified; wherever there is a generalization, although there are three phenomena, their meaning is already separated. Therefore, one knows that—
The nine [stages] are fixed as three; yet, regarding their separation and combination, this is actually discussed by way of selection.

This is the doctrine of separation and combination. As for the matter of selection, its principle remains constant: whether separated or combined, both selections pertain to the two types of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), taking the Middle Way as their essence.
This is what the Master of the *Ji* (Zhiyi) meant when he said that "both take the Dharma-body. Siming, however, stated that "each selects from the Empty and the Provisional. This is because...
The left and right manifest one another. Now, since these statements all take the Dharma-body as their standard, is this not taking the three Dharma-bodies from within the Nature?
Since it is said that each selects the empty and the provisional, is this not selecting the remaining six dharmas from within the nine?

If we follow their categories and speak of them in synthesis, then the three bodies are but a single body; the three principles and the three functions likewise each merge into one. Otherwise, it would not be so.
What is meant by "taking all" while simultaneously "discerning each"? The reason for this is that the *tǐ* (essence/nature) serves as the fundamental substance and the sovereign;
as such, the essence is the single ultimate, which does not encompass other meanings. Other meanings are its cultivation (*xiū*) and its function (*yòng*).

Whether they be the virtues of the rational nature (*lǐxìng*) or the manifest phenomena of cultivation (*xiūxiǎn*), these do not constitute the so-called oneness of the essential nature itself. This applies even to the nature of sentient beings.

The source is the fundamental principle of all Buddhas, which is likewise nothing other than the single nature (*ekadhātu*). This does not mean that when separated one practices both [nature and practice], while when combined one takes only nature;

regarding a comprehensive treatise on a single dispensation (*ekayāna*), the textual intent and the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) ought logically to encompass all aspects; thus, it employs the sevenfold two truths (*saptavidha-satya*).

Although this is a general indication, its true intent is actually to manifest the *Dharmatā-sūtra* as the King of Sūtras. Therefore, after demonstrating the entire dispensation in the text, it then says:

Indeed, regarding the comprehensive inclusion of the characteristics of the Dharma, there is nothing that surpasses this in terms of encompassing both the direct [teachings] and the transitional [teachings].

If it were not for this meaning, how could it be shown to be the "King of Sūtras" among all the sūtras of a single dispensation? Therefore, it is said: "Such an elucidation of the sūtra gathers the entirety of the transformation [of beings] within it, leaving nothing unexhausted.

It is also said: "The various divisions of the teachings of a single dispensation are equal within these sections. Thus, we know that while the indication is general, its specific application lies elsewhere.
Among these, it is clarified by this: if we now discuss the entire dispensation as a whole, the teaching of the sevenfold two-truths (sapta-dvaya-satya) is indeed influential.

Nevertheless, this should merely be understood as a general, broad reconciliation; it does not necessarily mean that the three sets of three dharmas-phenomena (tri-tri-dharma-lakṣaṇa) are entirely identical to the sevenfold two-truths.

Regarding the meaning of the "separate connection" (bie jietong): although the explanatory text (*jìwén*) provides a detailed analysis, answering in accordance with the question, it ultimately remains difficult to reconcile. Furthermore, it says:

"Moreover, within the text, there is no explicit statement that 'there are seven kinds of two truths. This is precisely the point. This is a teaching common to the entire lifetime of the Buddha’s ministry.

Regarding the teachings—whether in terms of their phrasing or their principles—are these not the three conventional and the three ultimate?

Furthermore, in elucidating the perfect fusion of the three truths, wherein emptiness, the provisional, and the middle are identical, since both the phrasing and the principles are thus harmonized, are these not the three kinds of Middle Way? If one does not take these three as the King of Sutras, what else could one point to?
By interpreting it in this manner, the text will naturally become clear; why must one insist on limiting it to the seven or the two, thereby discarding [this approach]?

The scriptures that serve as the sovereign for various schools, and the sovereigns of those various schools, are no different from what is sovereign within the Radiance (Guangming).

Regarding the general framework of phenomena arising according to conditions (1, 2, 3, 12, 22, 26), the treatise states:
The One True Dharma-realm is fundamentally devoid of any trace or limit; yet, as the Great Universal Category, there is no phenomenon it does not encompass. Because it encompasses all...

Therefore, it transforms through perfuming; because of this transformation, it arises as a complete manifestation. Since arising and manifestation are mutually integrated, phenomena and principle are non-dual.
This is the Great Substance that accords with conditions as elucidated by our school; regarding the source of the dharmas of arising, nothing surpasses this.

However, while there are distinctions between defilement and purity according to how one accords with conditions, there is likewise a difference between the true and the false within the dharmas of arising. [When] acceding to conditions, [there is] defilement...
Regarding "purity," the teachings and principles are certainly in agreement; however, concerning the true and false nature of the dharmas that arise, there have long been divergent theories.

For instance, among the various masters who include the earth element [in their systems], they differ on whether there are eight or nine consciousnesses. Similarly, there are differences in their calculations regarding the true and false nature of the dharmas that arise. Tiantai refuted these views.

It is said that if one dogmatically adheres to the reality of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), one falls into the error of the primordial darkness (*ādikṛta*) giving rise to cognition, and the fault of conceptualizing the existence of self-nature and other-nature, and so forth.

However, the doctrine elucidated by our own school is not thus. For instance, because the essence of nature is utterly extinguished, when speaking from the perspective of one’s own practice (*svacaryā*) while remaining free from attachment, it is said:
"The mind we now clarify—whether as ignorance or non-ignorance—does not arise from itself; therefore, it should not be regarded as truly arising."
All dharmas do not arise from another, and therefore they are not false; they do not arise from both [self and other], and therefore they are not a conjunction of the real and the false;
they do not arise without cause, and therefore there is no so-called "arising" distinct from these three.

Although they do not arise from self, other, or the like, according to the gates of teaching, one may provisionally employ them for the sake of conversion; thus, there is no hindrance to the fourfold exposition, which is said to exist when there are the causes of the four *siddhāntas*.
The conditions may also be explained in this way: thus, one may speak of self-arising, or other-arising, or co-arising, or arising apart from causes.
If one speaks of self-arising, it means that the *dharmatā* gives rise to all phenomena. If one speaks of other-arising, it means that ignorance gives rise to all phenomena.
If one speaks of co-arising, it means that [ignorance and the *dharmatā* together give rise to them].

The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) arises through conjunction. If one were to speak of arising as being separate [from this], it would imply that neither ignorance nor the nature of phenomena exists, and that all phenomena arise spontaneously without such conjunction.

To speak in this manner does not contradict the principle above that all phenomena are devoid of separation, nor does it fall into the error below of a primordial darkness (*ādikṛta*), while also remaining consistent with the *siddhānta*.

The explanation regarding "being clothed by things" is merely its general meaning; yet, there is also a distinct meaning. Thus, in various texts, some state that all phenomena arise from the *dharmatā* (nature of reality);

It is simply that dharmas have strengths and weaknesses, and words have distinctions of subject and guest; in reality, however, they rely upon and await one another to fulfill the function of producing phenomena."

However, while it may be acceptable to sever the nine realms created by ignorance, if one were to sever the nine [realms] created by True Suchness (*tathatā*), would one not also sever True Suchness itself?

This is all the more so for the emptiness and the provisional that are cultivated during the distinct stages and practices; these are precisely the two causes—the object-condition (*ālambana-hetu*) and the enabling cause (*janaka-hetu*).

If the nine [grades of delusion] are severed sequentially, should the conditions (*pratyaya*) and causes (*hetu*) also be severed? If the conditions and causes are severed, how can this manifest the "correct" [teaching]?

Furthermore, why is it said that only when the nine are exhausted are the conditions and causes said to be fully complete? The answer is: these are all difficulties raised by using the Perfect (*yuan*) to challenge the Distinct (*bie*).

Therefore, they serve as challenges within the gates of the teachings. If one grasps the underlying intent of the provisional (*quan*) and the real (*shi*), what difficulty could there be? This is because the teachings are provisional.

The nine realms (navadhātu) do not exist as inherent natures; thus, there is a sense in which they can be severed. However, according to the ultimate principle, there is no logical basis for severing them.
This differs from the "perfect teaching" (yuanquan), which points out that cultivated evil is itself the nature, and thus neither ignorance nor the nine realms are to be severed.

Nevertheless, in the Separate Teaching (biejiao), one severs the nine realms while not severing the conditions and causes (yuanliao). This is because the nine realms are themselves deluded defilement—the afflictions that obscure [the truth]—whereas the conditions and causes refer to...
The Buddha-realm is the cause capable of manifesting [the true nature]. Because it is not identical [to the nine realms], it is called "distinct cultivation.
Since this is the cause of Buddhahood, it is able to destroy the nine realms; yet, by means of destroying the nine, it manifests the conditions (pratyaya) and the understanding (pariniṣpanna).

Therefore, it is said that only when the nine are exhausted can the conditions and understanding be said to be fully complete. This record states it clearly: as it says, "Because within the Distinct Teaching there are no nine [realms] of inherent virtue."

The severance of both self and other can resolve the first difficulty. Furthermore, it is said: "By separately cultivating the conditions (yuan) and the realization (liao), one adorns the primordially existing, eternally abiding Dharmakāya.
This can resolve the second difficulty. Moreover, by further citing the *Miaozong* (The Subtle Pivot) to harmonize and explain this, the meaning becomes even more manifest.

Alas, those who are deluded are unable to employ these insights. Yet, is the fruit of the nine realms not destroyed? To answer: from the perspective of the essential substance (*ti*), the nine realms...

From the outset, there is no fixed dharma. As for the question of whether there is "destruction" or not, this merely concerns how one’s emotional understanding interprets the meaning expressed by the teachings;
it does not mean that [the Buddha-nature] is like a vessel that, once broken, can never be restored. That it may become manifest again after having been obscured is likewise a matter of principle.

Many people are confused about this, so I have briefly indicated it. Someone may ask: "In the *Wenju*, you establish three kinds of Buddha-realms within the Separate Teaching (pratyekabuddhayāna), etc."
How do these differ from [the concept of] "perfect" (yuan)? It is said: they are not the same. Within the perfect, the six [categories] are all Buddha; how could it be merely three types?

Furthermore, the reasons why they are called the Buddha of Principle-nature (*li-xing*) and so forth are even more different. Someone asked: regarding the four kinds of conditions—provisional (*yuan*), understanding (*liao*), and so on—how do they differ?
"The second [of these] is seen in the *Miaozong* (Profound Meaning). As for the remaining two, upon what texts do they rely? It is said: 'They exist in other texts.
Although their specific names are not explicitly stated here, they may nonetheless be subsumed under the various pairs of causes. Furthermore, it is said:

'Either the first is the object-condition (*ālambana*) and the second is the cognitive-perfection (*vijñapti*), or the first is the cognitive-perfection and the second is the object-condition'—this still refers to the aforementioned middle-and-extreme, emptiness-and-falsity. Thus, what is clarified here is the distinct [classification]."
Regarding the practice: to which of the four [categories] does it belong? It is said: it primarily pertains to the Middle and the Extremes (*madhyānta*), yet it also encompasses all four;

this can be understood from the text. Someone may ask: "The *Xuánmíng* (Profound Clarification) explains the phenomena and principle, the provisional and the real, and the primary and secondary dharmas in two layers.

Why, then, does the *Shìqian* (Sub-commentary) explain them by summarizing them into ignorance (*avidyā*) and the nature of reality (*dharmatā*)? It is said: Those phenomena and principles, when contrasted with the subsequent five categories—such as teaching, practice, and so forth—are both...

It belongs to the category of principle (*li*). Therefore, within the context of nature, it is explained in terms of both phenomena (*shi*) and principle. This is as when it is said that the "basis of non-abiding" is already pervasive;
since it pervades both ignorance (*avidyā*) and the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), both may serve as the basis. Thus, the term "Ultimate Truth" (*paramārtha-satya*) refers to principle;

it does not point solely to the dharma-nature, but also points to ignorance, for ignorance is itself the basis of principle. Consequently, the three thousand realms constitute its manifold manifestation.
"Luó" (羅) refers to what is called "the three thousand [realms] existing within principle," which are collectively termed ignorance (*avidyā*).

Someone may ask: "Now, you have cited the *Xuánwén* (玄文) to clarify the meaning of the object of contemplation in the Separate Teaching (*biéjiào*); what is the underlying intent being revealed? I reply: There are two points here.

First, it reveals that the *tathatā* (true thusness) of the Separate Teaching also encompasses all phenomena; however, because the teaching is provisional, it does not identify [true thusness] as being identical with the nine realms of existence. Therefore, it speaks only of its possessing "reality."

The passage beginning with "The Dharma is equal" (法等) clarifies the meaning of the distinct principle that accords with conditions; thus it says, "From this wondrous existence, all dharmas are produced.

This is merely a case of production, yet it does not differ from the Perfect [Teaching]. Someone may ask: "The *Miaojiji* (Record of the Wondrous) discriminates between the similarities and differences of the positions and phases.

The fact that worldly phenomena are eternally abiding has already been clarified in the *Benyiming shixiang changzhu* (Original Clarification of the Eternality of Worldly Phenomena), as explained in the *Jiyao* (Essential Points), and the *Miaozong* (Wondrous Canon) also clearly distinguishes and reveals this. Yet, as for the [sentient] mind..."
It is still not clear. For now, let us set aside the explanations regarding the characteristics of phenomena (*lakṣaṇa*) and directly reveal their essential purport.

It is said that the reason the world-phenomena (*saṃsāra-lakṣaṇa*) abide eternally is for no other reason than this: it is simply to clarify that all dharmas are fundamentally one. Because they are fundamentally one, one does not perceive any difference in terms of alternation or flux;

nor can one distinguish between nature and characteristics (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*), or between phenomena and principle (*dharma-tattva*). All such [distinctions] are merely the products of biased and gradualistic sentiments.
Seeing this, how does it relate to the discourse on the ultimate and wondrous state of perfect manifestation? One must understand its principle;

let me attempt to illustrate it with a simple analogy. It is just like a single breath that permeates the four seasons: all things are born from this single breath and grow through this single breath.
As for withering and decay, they too are entirely one *qi* (vital energy). Because they exist within the state of withering and decay, there is nowhere that is not one *qi*;
thus, there is nowhere that is not eternal. The *Lotus Sūtra* relies upon this to directly demonstrate what is called the "oneness of principle" (*li-yi*) and what is called "ultimate equality.

These are all its essential points. Only by understanding this can one know the meaning of the *Wondrous Commentary*'s doctrine that there is only arising and only abiding, as stated in the *Awakening of Faith*.
That which is called the "four characteristics" exist simultaneously. An ancient master said, "When it perishes, it follows along with others.

A former sage further said, "When it perishes, it perishes along with others; therefore, it is eternally imperishable. (This is entirely identical in meaning to the ancient master’s intent, differing only in its added commentary. Is this not precisely that principle? Someone asked:

"The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary on the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*) cites passages from the *Laṅkāvatāra Mahā-śāstra*; is it not solely for the purpose of clarifying the meaning of 'following conditions' (*suíyuán*)?"
"However, is there also a difference in meaning? He replied, "There is. It does not go beyond the meaning of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).

Thus, in the *Laṅkāvatāra*, [the teaching] arises from within oneself; in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it enters from without. Since both causes and conditions are complete, the principle of 'following conditions' (*anupratyaya*) is all the more manifest;

one should know that citing these proofs is by no means trivial. Someone asked: "Regarding the two types of cultivation—contrary and conforming—and the two stages of arising, what are their similarities and differences?"
How so? It is said that what is different is named as the same, and what is the same is contrasted with the different;

thus, it is not one-sided. This is because the two types of cultivation are discussed in terms of delusion and awakening. Furthermore, they are distinguished as having only two modes of arising, as this follows the sequence of teaching and practice.

Each, moreover, encompasses the ten kinds of threefold dharmas; this constitutes their difference. Yet, they may also be mutually integrated, such that there is progress in one and failure in the other; thus, it is also...
The same applies to difference. Now, one should perform a fourfold analysis (*catuṣkoṭi*). That is to say: (3) that which is cultivated in reverse order, but does not arise in reverse order;
(4) that which arises in reverse order, but is not cultivated in reverse order; (2) that which is cultivated in forward order and arises in forward order;

and (1) that which is neither cultivated in reverse order nor arises in reverse order. Thus, the continuation of the *Yihui* [Treatise] is as follows; the essential points of the *Zhiyao yihui* [Essential Summary of the Treatise] are as follows:
They are all inferior to the first phrase and do not fully express the meaning of the fourfold proposition; this can be understood by comparing them. Someone may ask:

regarding the passage in the *Yijiao* (Pointing to the Essentials) which states, "Our school clarifies the essence of the three thousand [realms]," there are three difficulties arising from this single line: first, the difficulty that principle (*li*) would possess differentiation;

second, the difficulty that [the essence] would not follow conditions (*yuan*); and third, the difficulty that there would be differentiation even when ignorance (*avidyā*) is removed. (Thus it is said.)

(Question: If that is so, then for those who now speak on behalf of the Four Ming Mountains, if one were to provide an exegesis to resolve this, it would be no difficulty provided one grasps the underlying intent as explained above.
In short, the reason for pointing to this essential point is to manifest the principle of our own school (*jia*) wherein the essence and its manifestations are non-dual.
Thus, regardless of whether one conforms or does not conform [to the teachings], nor does one discuss the distinction between delusion and enlightenment, from beginning to end.

Because the "constant" is that which is constantly complete, the three thousand dharmas are each perfectly manifest. To further illustrate this teaching with a single phrase, one will then know that the principles and patterns have a basis.
As the *Famen* (Gate of Non-duality) states: "When the three thousand exist in principle, they are collectively termed ignorance."

The three thousand [dharmas] are both constant and possess both essence and function. Is this not what is meant by saying that the essence of the three thousand gives rise to the function of the three thousand according to conditions?
Furthermore, it is said: "When the three thousand are perfected as fruition, they are all termed 'Eternal Bliss. Eternal Bliss is the return to the source of the fruition-merit.
Is this not the fact that when not following conditions, the three thousand are perfectly manifest? It is further said: "The three thousand undergo no change."
Ignorance (*avidyā*) is itself enlightenment (*vidyā*). Since it is already enlightenment, there is no longer any ignorance; is this not the removal of ignorance through differentiation?
Yet this differentiation is itself non-differentiation, for it is only in contrast to that state of pure, undifferentiated unity.

Thus, by means of non-differentiation, one distinguishes through differentiation. Therefore, the text says: "The principle-body is without difference," and further: "The ground possesses both peach and plum."
And so forth. Furthermore, it is said that "that which remains unchanged from beginning to end" can, in our view, be subsumed under no more than three meanings:

the meaning of formal opposition (*xingdui*), the meaning of mutual identity (*xiangji*), and the meaning of essential nature (*tixing*). (As elaborated at length. Although there are these three meanings, their principle does not follow divergent paths; one thread runs through them all, collectively manifesting the perfect teaching (*yuanzhi*).

As for those who specifically raise the objection regarding the "mutual displacement" (*xingduo*) of phenomena and principle, this is certainly not the case when one reaches the point of analytical discernment.
To simply summarize it in terms of the Three Truths and explain it through such distinctions is likewise not correct.

This not only fails to resolve the opponent's difficulties, but also reveals the bias of one who has turned their back on the fundamental tenets; indeed, the seeds of this [error] were sown here. Someone asked:

"The *Miaojiji* states that the various teachings are distinguished by whether they are 'identical' (*ji*) or 'not identical' (*bujì*). Since the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*) properly corresponds to 'not identical,' why was the previous [criticism] directed at the Separate Teaching?"
Furthermore, you admit that "identity" (*ji*) is the same as [the principle]. Yet, does the treatise follow conditions? Moreover, the *Yiyao* states:

"One should know that when it does not discuss 'inherent possession' (*liju*), it must use 'possession' to manifest 'identity' (*jixianji*) in order for the meaning of the Perfect [Teaching] to be established. If it were merely identity without possession, it would be nothing more than a partial meaning.
Does this not contradict the text of the *Miaojiji* as well? Furthermore, since you have already admitted that "possession" is used to manifest "identity," why...
One might object: "Since it is already shown that [the distinct] possesses [the inclusive], does this not cause the distinct to belong to the inclusive according to conditions? The reply is:

When the distinct is said not to be identical [to the inclusive], this is a statement made by distinguishing the distinct from the inclusive through their forms. Even when discussing the distinct itself, from the perspective of its actual principle, it is not that this meaning does not exist.

Now, regarding the principles of "bestowing" (*yǔ*) and "withdrawing" (*duó*) clarification: to bestow it means that one attains [the meaning] immediately; this refers to the texts that fully indicate the essential points.
To withdraw it means that [the meaning] is already complete [in what precedes]; this refers to the texts that are not the subtle records (*miào jì*).

One may also bestow and withdraw them by halves. The cases of bestowing in full and withdrawing in full are distinct; although there is no principle of bestowing in full, other texts should also possess this quality, though they are simply not presented together here.

The text states: As it is said, although the central [state] does not fully contain the nine realms of the environment and its inhabitants (*āśraya-adhiṣṭhāna*), it is not that the wondrous form and wondrous mind of the Buddha-realm are absent;
how could this not also be called "possessing" them? If one further discusses the principle of "possessing," it likewise does not go beyond three meanings:

first, mutual non-identity; second, mutual manifestation; and third, mutual identity. (As explained at length... Just as in the case of following conditions (*pratyaya-anuvartana*), one knows [the realms] through their identity.
It is not that they lack [the other attributes], but merely that they are mutually exclusive. Regarding the basis for this discussion, it is precisely to manifest their mutual possession.
As for the latter two meanings, if they pertain to our own school, they may be found in the sūtras and śāstras; this is because one may first preserve the general principles therein.

As explained in that commentary: if it were not explicitly stated, how could such a thing exist? Someone may ask: The *Ten Gates of Non-duality* states, "In turbid water and clear water, the waves and moisture are no different.

How does this compare to the meaning of "the unchanging following conditions" as explained in the *Zangshu* (Commentary on the *Treatise on the Five Teachings*), which says that the nature of non-change does not obstruct the arising of waves, and although the waves undergo ten thousand movements, they do not obstruct the single moisture? Therefore, movement and stillness are... [no difference].

Second: What difference is there between the phenomena? If they were different, by what means could they be distinguished? If they were not different, they would merely follow conditions without being distinct. It is said:
To understand the characteristics of difference, one should take the essential passages and examine them.

For example, it is said that "waves" are a metaphor for the three thousand [worlds] as the simultaneous function, while "moisture" is a metaphor for the three thousand [worlds] as the simultaneous essence. One must know that within the defiled state, although the water is turbid, it is nonetheless entirely moisture.
It is the wave itself. When it is clear, how could there be a separate moisture from the wave? Therefore, it is said that there is no distinction.

Using this to evaluate that, one will finally know that the commentaries and sub-commentaries have not exhausted its essential meaning. Furthermore, as the *Yiyao* says: "Thus we know that the ultimate perfection of other schools merely speaks of 'the arising of nature' (*xingqi*)."

It does not speak of "inherent possession" (*xingju*); this is deeply worthy of contemplation. Precisely because it does not speak of inherent possession, the nature (*xing*) and phenomena (*shi*) are distinct.

When one reaches the state of "identical with principle" (*jili*), one must negate their differentiation so as to return to the single nature; thus, individual dharmas cannot remain perfectly distinct.

This is how it differs from the Perfect [Teaching]. Someone may ask: The *Yizao* (Essentials) further states that if one does not discuss the "embodiment of the essence" (*ti-ju*), then regarding "following conditions" (*suiyuan*) and...

"Following conditions" (*suiyuan*) pertains entirely to the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*). Yet, the Separate Teaching also possesses the principle of "not following conditions. How can it be asserted definitively that the separate principle follows conditions? [The author] replies:

This is merely a provisional explanation, as the text specifically clarifies this point for the time being. The dharmas produced by the *ālayavijñāna* do not constitute the True Suchness (*tathatā*) following conditions.
To speak from a second perspective: the dharmas produced by deluded consciousness (*wangshi*) are not distinct from True Suchness. Therefore, regarding the purport of the teaching—
It is the same. Someone asked: "The 'Analysis of Difficulties in Ten Gates' (*Shimen xinan*) is already a discourse for supporting the school;

why not now adopt it and instead establish your own theory regarding the clarification of the school's tenets and the analysis of difficulties? He replied: "As for those who support the school, there is none among them who does not think thus.
Yet, when one examines their explanations, many deviate from the principles of reality and are often erroneous in their judgments of right and wrong. However, based on the present..."
Examine it with your own mind; its truth or falsehood can thus be known. Someone asked: "To whom did the 'Twenty Questions on Following Conditions' (Suíyuán èrshí wèn) originally belong?
Furthermore, are the questions attributed to National Teacher An the same as those of our present school, or are they different? Having raised this question:

"Should one provide an answer? He replied: "The emergence of this question has both a general and a specific sense. Generally, it is directed at those who do not believe in the principle of following conditions (*pratyaya*).
Specifically, however, it is intended solely for the Master [Sengzhao] and his inquiry. To analyze the difficulty: the Master once formulated twenty questions."
This is precisely what [Zhi]yi intended to refute when he addressed the Master of Qi.

As for the National Teacher An, although he was a disciple of the Master of Qi, his underlying intent in formulating the question actually accords with that of Siming, as seen in the text of the inquiry. The meaning of the text is not obscure;
it is simply that each side established its own thesis, seeing only one perspective. If one wishes to provide an answer, it should be done exactly as in the *Golden Needle*.

Regarding the forty-six questions set forth, a single answer would have sufficed; however, here we merely accept the principle that individual principles follow conditions, which effectively answers twenty of those questions.
Otherwise, each and every question must be meticulously analyzed and resolved. Or, as for the questions:

According to the "Chapter on Harmonization," the *Awakening of Faith* (Qixin lun) is comprehensive across the three teachings (*sanjiao*), whereas the *Zangshu* (Commentary on the Tripitaka) is restricted solely to the distinct teaching (*biejiao*).

This is clear from the text’s reasoning. Why, then, do some commentators still claim that Siming refuted the *Awakening of Faith* as being of the distinct teaching? It is said that there is a reason for this.
Namely, Gushan once remarked that Siming held the view that the *Awakening of Faith* was like a whale being swallowed whole; since then, this has been transmitted [as such].

This serves merely as a pretext for verbal debate. One fails to realize that the phrase "names and forms arising in accordance with conditions" (suiyuan mingxiang) originally derives from the *Zangshu* (Commentary on the [Avataṃsaka] Sūtra).

How can one allow the entire explanation to be invalidated simply because of a deficiency in the interpreter's understanding? Thus, once the judgment is established, it follows that "arising in accordance with conditions" belongs specifically to the distinct teaching (bieming).

Chapter Four: The Theory of Habitual Tendencies (*vāsanā*).
The General Introduction to the Upper Discourse states: Delusions also have many names; among them, one is "habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*).

Habitual tendencies are fundamentally not the primary afflictions themselves, yet there are those who speak of them as being the "primary afflictions," those who speak of them in contrast to the "primary afflictions," and those who speak of them in relation to the "primary afflictions. Now, this treatise...
These correspond to the latter two examples. Since they are discussed in relation to the primary afflictions (*kleśa*), they lack an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of their own;

rather, they arise as derivative forces (*vāsana*) from the primary delusions, which is what is meant by "continuing habitually" from the preceding state. Thus it is said: "The derivative forces produced by the repeated cultivation of afflictions;
because they are the force of habituation," which precisely captures this meaning. It is, for example, like feet that have been bound for a long time, or like the clothes of a nursing mother.

It is like a vessel filled with incense; or [if it is empty], it is like a faint wisp of smoke. It is like a small amount of salt cast into a great river. Such is the nature of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
Originally, they are based on the principle of the single true nature (*ekadharmatā*), which is fundamentally luminous and fundamentally pure.

How, then, could there be any delusive defilement? It is simply that although this principle is fundamentally luminous, in reality it has never been [separately] luminous; and although its nature is fundamentally pure, in reality...
Because they have never been purified, there exist therein defilements of delusion and habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). Thus, when categorized vertically, there are three:

namely, the delusions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), the delusions of the sands of dust (*rajas*), and the delusions of ignorance (*avidyā*). When categorized horizontally, there are likewise three: namely, greed (*lobha*), anger (*dveṣa*), and delusion (*moha*). When summarized, there are also three:
namely, afflictions (*kleśa*), hindrances (*āvaraṇa*), and delusions (*bhrānti*). As for what are called "coverings" (*nīvaraṇa*), "entanglements" (*paryavasthāna*), and...

Terms such as "outflows" (āsrava), "bonds" (bandhana), "fettering" (saṃyojana), and "dust-like toil" (kleśa) are all manifestations of delusional defilement; they are merely different names for various ways of opening and closing [the categories].

Thus, although the delusions within principle are numerous, they do not differ from being mere falsehoods. Although the habitual tendencies of these delusions are numerous, they do not differ from being mere secondary divisions.
If one knows that falsehood is not reality, one will necessarily comprehend the means by which falsehood is destroyed.
This is the essential point. If one knows that the remaining portions are difficult to eliminate, then one will recognize the fundamental reason for severing the habit-energies (*vāsanā*).

This is the specific school’s subtle intention in discussing the habit-energies of delusion. However, since delusions have both general and particular aspects, their names and characteristics must be distinguished.

Since habit-energies have both small and great degrees, their meanings must be differentiated. When discussing severance within the stages of perfect realization (*yuanwei*), there are distinctions regarding presence and absence, as well as progress and regression.
Regarding these differences, the indications of their textual characteristics reveal distinctions in preference and inclination.

As for the engagement of the various teaching gates, there are such discussions as the "supporting of habits" versus the "overcoming of habits," as well as the meanings of "simultaneous severance" and "perfect severance. All of these have been subjects of debate since ancient times.
Since it is essential that this not remain obscure, I shall therefore discuss it here.

Within the separate categories, there are forty-six instances of texts concerning the class of *vāsanā* (habitual tendencies). Among these, nine concern the names and characteristics of the fundamental afflictions (*mūlakleśa*) of the three delusions.

There are five categories in total: twelve [passages] concerning the differences in *vāsanā* (habitual tendencies) according to the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna; eight [passages] clarifying whether the elimination of *vāsanā* occurs at the stage of perfect enlightenment and whether there is progress or not;
seven [passages] where the text points out that the "knots of habitual tendencies" have both general and specific aspects, as well as similarities and differences;
and ten [passages] demonstrating the severance of correct and habitual tendencies, where the text involves other related meanings. These constitute the five types.
Section on the Names and Characteristics of the Active Defilements (*paryavasthāna*) of the Three Delusions (6, 9, 10, 13, 14, 16, 17, 20).

The Treatise says: The difference between the active defilements (*paryavasthāna*) and their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) lies in their being the root and the branch. If one does not first clarify the arrival at the root, what can be said regarding the branches?
What are called the "active defilements" are the three delusions. Now, the root of delusion is not fixed as three; it is categorized as such based on the Truths (*satya*) that are obstructed.

Regarding the characteristics of the principle-dharma (*li-faxiang*), it is said here that there are three; hence it is stated: "Viewing and affliction (*jiansi*) obstruct the empty stillness," and again:

"The common and specific [aspects of] viewing and affliction obstruct ultimate emptiness" (this latter point differs slightly and shall be distinguished later). Now, returning to the three delusions (*sanhuo*), their various names and characteristics have many different categories of meaning.
Ten points are used to clarify them: first, regarding how they are named, there are those named from their [respective] understandings and those named from... [the text continues].

Regarding the naming [of afflictions] based on their essential nature (*tattva*) as opposed to what they obstruct: for example, the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) are named according to both their essence and their manifestation; the delusions of thought (*bhāvanā-kleśa*) are named solely according to their manifestation, following this same principle.
Ignorance (*avidyā*), however, is named according to its essence; the "dust-like" delusions (*rajas-kleśa*) are named according to what they obstruct.

Furthermore, while the three types of delusion are collectively termed "ignorance," there is a distinction between the branches and the root. They are collectively termed "lack of knowledge" (*ajñāna*), yet there is a distinction between the defiled and the non-defiled. They are collectively termed "view" (*dṛṣṭi*).

Regarding "thought" (*vitarka*), there are distinctions between the general and the specific; thus, the basis from which it derives its name can be inferred by analogy, and it is not uniform in all cases.

Second, from the perspective of the characteristics of the afflictions (*kleśa*), within both the internal and external realms, there are those that are associated (*saṃprayukta*) and those that are independent (*svatantra*).

That is to say, "associated" refers to those that conjoin with the various latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), while "independent" refers to those that merely obstruct the principle directly. Third, from the perspective of their sequential arising:

First is ignorance (*avidyā*), followed by the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*). This is as described in the *Awakening of Faith* regarding the sequential arising of the three subtleties and six grossnesses.

Since the "dust-sand" [afflictions] are fundamentally not delusions, they are not included therein. Fourth, according to the principle of the sequence of what is to be severed, the dust-sand afflictions are the reverse of the aforementioned;
although they do not nourish rebirth, they obstruct transformation and guidance. Therefore, they are severed after the afflictions of views and thought. If one looks toward the Truth...
The transformation of skillful means is because it takes ignorance as its own root and branch. Fifth, from the perspective of the phenomena and principles that are obstructed:

view-delusion (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) and afflictive delusion (*kleśa-avidyā*) obstruct principle, while the delusions of dust and sand (*rajas-aṇu-avidyā*) obstruct phenomena. Furthermore, discussing view-delusion and afflictive delusion themselves: view-delusion obstructs principle.
6. Regarding the objects obstructed by thought (*cetanā*): as it is said, "violation of principle arises from views (*dṛṣṭi*), while the retribution of results arises from thought.

7. From the perspective of the person who can sever them: views and thoughts are severed by all three vehicles, and are therefore called "common delusions" (*sāmānya-kleśa*). The *rajas-resembling-sand* (*rajas-tulya*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) are severed only by Bodhisattvas, and are therefore called "distinctive delusions" (*viśeṣa-kleśa*).

8. From the perspective of the realm (*dhātu*) upon which they depend: views and thoughts constitute the delusions within the realm (*dhātu-kleśa*), and are thus collectively termed the "four abodes" (*catvāraḥ sthitayaḥ*). The *rajas-resembling-sand*...
Ignorance (*avidyā*) is a defilement outside the realms; therefore, it constitutes a separate dwelling (*vihāra*).

If one were to establish three dwellings for each [of the other categories] by analogy with the external, then the names of the four dwellings would apply only to the internal realms according to their classification in the teachings. Thus, generally they pertain only to the internal realms, while specifically they pertain only to the external realms.

If the specific [dwellings] were connected to the external realms, there would be only ignorance, and one could no longer further open up the four dwellings. The eight [defilements] arise from moistening rebirth.

Moistening birth refers to how the afflictions of view (*dṛṣṭi*), thought (*saṃjñā*), and ignorance (*avidyā*) can moisten birth both within and outside the realms. The *rajas* (dust-like) afflictions do not moisten birth.

Furthermore, even if they were to moisten it, the residual habit-energies (*vāsanā*) do not moisten it. Regarding the nine [categories] through the opening and closing of the general and specific, there are four permutations:

namely, opening the general while closing the specific, as in the five stages of dwelling (*pañca-vihāra*); opening the specific while closing the general, as in the three delusions; and opening both the general and the specific, each of which has its own...

Regarding the categories of afflictions, both the general and the specific are combined together, as was done with the two preceding delusions; by grouping them in this way, none are left unaccounted for. As for the ten [delusions] derived from metaphors:
it is said that the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) are like forty *li* of water, while the delusions of thought (*bhāvanā-kleśa*) are like a single drop of water.

Furthermore, the delusions of view and thought are like oil upon water, whereas ignorance (*avidyā*) is like milk within water. If one integrates these three types of delusions according to the teachings to harmonize the general and the specific, then the text...

There is the analogy of cutting scallions and peeling scallions; this refers to what is sequential and what is non-sequential. Thus, while the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) have already been clarified, the essence (*svabhāva*) remains unmanifest.

Although many previous [masters] have spoken on this, I shall now state that there are both similarities and differences. The similarity lies in the fact that they are all but a single deluded mind, yet they are distinguished by the three types of affliction (*kleśa*).

Therefore, ignorance (*avidyā*) takes the failure to comprehend the mind and its attachment to the two extremes as its essence. As for the dust-and-sand-like afflictions (*rajas-tulya-kleśa*), [they take... as their essence.

Those of inferior wisdom do not understand that all phenomena have as their essence [the nature of emptiness]. They perceive and conceptualize with outflow-tainted minds, taking the attachment to the six sense objects as their essence.
Although there are other explanations, they do not go beyond this.
Regarding the differences in the examples of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) according to the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna: (4, 8, 11, 12, 19, 23, 24).
[29] [32] [42] [45] [46]. The Treatise says: Generally, among all the scriptural teachings, there are many instances where the term "habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*) is mentioned.
For example, regarding the "correct habitual tendencies" (*samyag-vāsanā*) of the Hīnayāna, their explanation is always fixed.
Even if they hear the Mahāyāna teaching concerning habitual tendencies, based on their own respective level, they merely refer to them as "habitual tendencies" alone, and do not...
One knows that these are the sands of dust, ignorance, the household, and identity.

Because the small covers the large, or the large is used to indicate the small, the fundamental afflictions and their habitual tendencies are presented alternately according to the great teachings; thus, it is sometimes said that the tendencies are severed, and sometimes it is said they are not severed.
Nevertheless, all [explanations] follow the specific textual passages; their applications each accord with their respective meanings, and from the outset there has been no fixed doctrine.

Precisely because there has never been a fixed doctrine, one should know that the theory of *vāsanā* (habitual tendencies) cannot be stated in a general manner, nor should one adhere to a single passage or a single meaning.
This is like comparing arrows and stones. For if the *anuśaya* (latent tendency) were the fruit, how could the *kleśa* (active affliction) be further designated as the *vāsanā* (habitual tendency)?
And if the *vāsanā* were the fruit, how could the *kleśa* be further designated as the *anuśaya*? If there were definitely a *vāsanā* to be severed, one should not say that there is no severing;
if there were definitely no *vāsanā*, one should likewise not say that there is severing. If we examine its nature through what is severed...

That which is not severed: by examining what exists through that which does not exist, one finds that what is said to exist is not necessarily existent, and what is said to be non-existent is not necessarily non-existent.
What is called "habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*) is not necessarily distinct from "active afflictions" (*kleśa*), and what is called "active afflictions" is not necessarily not habitual tendencies.

By this, one knows that their textual characteristics are fundamentally interpenetrating and cannot be reduced to a single identity. Nevertheless, while their names may be interchangeable, their essential natures (*tattva*) must not be conflated.
The phrasing may differ, but the principle cannot be altered. One must necessarily rely on the essential purport of the teachings to rectify the main path;

thus, the explanation will certainly attain certainty. Why is this? For instance, regarding ignorance and the dust-and-sand [afflictions], although they are explained in the Mahāyāna teachings as being essentially the primary afflictions (*āsrava*), they conceal the characteristics of the Hīnayāna and cannot be said to be distinct delusions.
If one were to know that there are distinct delusions, then one must also know that...

This is because it would contradict other principles; therefore, it is called "habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*). If one does not obscure these characteristics and speaks according to the great reality, they are in fact reduced to the "active afflictions" (*paryavasthāna*).

Thus it is said, and so forth. Furthermore, for a person of the Perfect Teaching whose faculties are sharp, hindrances are light, and whose contemplative practice is superior, how could there be habitual tendencies existing apart from the severed active afflictions, as is the case in the Lesser Vehicle?
It is only because of the application [of terminology] according to the specific textual passages that, at times, [the term is used].

It is also said that "habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are severed," as has been stated at length. Now, therefore, I shall explain this: according to the literal text, such may exist; yet according to principle, they do not. Why is this so?

Consider, for example, the three vehicles of the Lesser Teaching (*hīnayāna*): do their habitual tendencies have an end or not? There is a distinction between those that are undermined and those that are not.

It is not that there are no three vehicles; rather, their faculties vary between sharp and dull, and their contemplations vary between superior and inferior. Thus, while Śrāvakas sever only the active afflictions (*kleśa*), their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) remain entirely intact.
For Pratyekabuddhas, these habitual tendencies are somewhat attenuated compared to the former, which is why it is said they "infringe upon" the tendencies, though this does not imply a fixed limit.
As for Bodhisattvas, their faculties are sharp and their contemplation is superior; consequently, [the tendencies] no longer remain at all. It is on this basis that the previous statement was made.

It is said that [afflictions] are severed instantaneously; based on this, the distinctions between the three vehicles are established. However, from the perspective of the Bodhisattva, there is in reality no duality.

Using the small vehicle as a comparison for the great, it is clear that in the Perfect and Sudden teaching there is no further cultivation (*xi*). This principle is evident. Furthermore, according to the Perfect Teaching, even regarding the "correct" afflictions (*zhengshi*), the three delusions cannot admit of any difference;

how much less could there be a distinction in essence between the correct afflictions and their residual habits (*zhengxi*)? The words of Gushan are correct. As it is said regarding the realms (*jie*):...

The external [view] sees that since the afflictions of thought (*vitarka*) and deliberation (*vicāra*) have no distinct substance, how could their residual habits (*vāsanā*) possibly differ? Now, in this teaching, there is indeed much to be taken from it;

yet, among the former masters of old who spoke of the three schools and two identities, they were further confused by divergent interpretations, failing to properly distinguish what to adopt and what to reject.
All of these fail to investigate the fundamental beginning and end of the doctrinal intent, merely using names and characteristics to divide them.

It is simply a matter of distinction. Speaking in terms of the present: regarding the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), they certainly exist according to the teachings of the Hīnayāna.
