Regarding the habitual tendencies of the separate delusions (*pṛthag-moha*), they do not necessarily exist when speaking from the perspective of the Mahāyāna. As for these "immediate" habitual tendencies, one should merely discuss them by alternating between the Great and Small Vehicles;
there is no need for other explanations. Yet some, due to a mind indolent toward transforming and guiding others, [regard] them as being like the *rajas-aṃśu* (dust-like) delusions.

"Habituation" refers to the repeated arising of a mind attached to extremes; this constitutes the habituation of ignorance. All of these are merely conventional explanations passed down through tradition;
they are not necessarily so.
The Examples of Whether or Not There Is Progress or Regression in the Severing of Habit-Energies (*vāsanā*) within the Perfect Stage (21, 26, 27, 28, 36, 37, 38, 41).

The Treatise says: Regarding the discussion of the great habit-energies, only the Perfect [Vehicle] possesses what are called the stages of severance, as well as the existence or non-existence of progress or regression regarding these habit-energies.

Regarding the doctrine of "habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*), it is essential to make a definitive judgment and establish the correct standard. As stated in the *Gimingji* (Record of the Radiance) by Siming:

"The fundamental afflictions (*mūlakleśa*) of the Shared [Vehicle] are exhausted at the seventh stage of faith (*śraddhā*) in the Perfect [Teaching]; as for habitual tendencies, they persist until Buddhahood, wherein both shared and distinct tendencies are exhausted.

Later scholars critiqued this, claiming that it fails to encompass both the horizontal and vertical aspects [of delusion]. I, however, maintain that this precisely captures the Perfect Teaching’s exhaustion of both horizontal and vertical delusions.

[The Master] said: "Why do you, on the contrary, claim that [the afflictions] are not subsumed? If one were to say merely that the pervasive afflictions are exhausted through the seventh stage of the Perfect Teaching, this would only indicate vertical progression (*ūrdhva*).
Therefore, by taking the residual habits (*vāsanā*)—whether common or specific—and exhausting them together, one reveals that while it is vertical, it is not merely vertical.

If one were to stop at what is explained later, this would only indicate horizontal progression (*tiryak*). By returning to the previous principle to complete it, one reveals that while it is horizontal..."
It is neither horizontal nor vertical; thus, the principle of "perfect severance" (yuánduàn) is manifested.

Furthermore, in order to explain the passage concerning the simultaneous exhaustion of both the fundamental afflictions (*zhèng*) and their residual habits (*xí*), it is necessary to distinguish between the general and the specific, such that each may possess its own fundamental afflictions and residual habits.

However, since the Perfect Teaching (*yuán*) has no doctrine of residual habits belonging to its own [specific] family, it takes the sense of "dust-like sands" (*chénshā*) as the general residual habits, stating: "Because our school [regards] the residual habits of the Lesser Vehicle as the fourfold discrimination..."

Because there are forty-six categories [of afflictions]. This is explained entirely in accordance with the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary). "Specific cultivation" (*bie xi*) refers specifically to the ignorance (*avidyā*) of the subsequent stages;

hence it is said, "The ten stages sever the habit-energies (*vāsanā*) of craving," and so forth. As for what is called "specific delusions," they consist of forty-two categories, and their stages of severance are as usual.

This correctly states that in the Perfect Teaching (*yuan jiao*), there are no habit-energies. Furthermore, it says: "The habit-energies are fully explained as set forth in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra-ṭīkā*."

Thus, one takes the passage cited by him as proof. Therefore, it is known that, generally speaking, both the primary and habitual aspects of names and words each have their respective primary and habitual [correspondences], which is clear.
Now, since the "habitual" (*xi*) of the specific [aspect] is pointed out as that which is severed in the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), it is known to have no separate substance;
it refers back to ignorance (*avidyā*) itself as the habit. Otherwise, there would be a habit without a primary [correspondence], which is not logical. This is why... [the dust].

Regarding "the sands of the Ganges" (*sāhasra*) and the exhaustion of distinct practices: the obscurations of the sands of the Ganges pertain to phenomena (*dharma*), while the obscuration of ignorance pertains to principle (*li*).

Since the sudden and perfect [teachings] regarding phenomena and principle cannot be differentiated, if the principle has not yet been fully investigated and manifested, the phenomena likewise have not been exhausted; conversely, if the phenomena are exhausted, the principle must be fully investigated and manifested.
This is why the sands of the Ganges are exhausted at the time when the distinct [teachings] regarding principle are fully investigated and manifested. The purport of this meaning is subtle.
The esoteric [teachings] should not be known by those who study in a superficial manner; therefore, I am able to reveal them.
Regarding the luminous phrases and sentences, whether they be categorized as "universal" (*tong*) or "particular" (*bie*), their ultimate consummation resides entirely within the Buddha’s own words.

Guishan considered this to be a general exposition preceding the specific details, whereas Siming stated that upon reaching the stage of Buddhahood, not only do the particular aspects reach their limit, but the universal aspects also exhaust their boundaries. I now say that those who merely follow the literal text...

This is easy to see. The theory of Gushan is incorrect; it is difficult for those who investigate principle to understand. The theory of Siming is correct. Now, by simply clarifying what is correct, what is incorrect can be known. Why is this?
It is because, in the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*), the discussion of the *darśana-heya* and *bhāvanā-heya* afflictions must encompass both the beginning and the end, being both horizontal and vertical.
The principle that serves as the object of obstruction is ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*), which pervades all places; therefore, it causes the [afflictions] to...
Obstructions also pervade the ten directions. Thus, that which is severed at the stage of the causal ground is not only not yet exhausted;

furthermore, the views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) of subsequent stages, as well as the pervasive delusions of the ten directions, have not yet been fully eradicated. Therefore it is said: "It is because of [the presence of] views and afflictions, etc.

Consequently, "pervading the worlds of the ten directions" is spoken in terms of the horizontal (transcendental) dimension, while "not yet exhausted at the causal stage" is spoken in terms of the vertical (temporal) progression. Furthermore, it is said: "The six..."

Regarding the statement that "sentient beings are equal," this is still explained in terms of the boundaries of *dṛṣṭi* (views) and *kleśa* (afflictions); thus, the general does not preclude the particular.
Therefore, it is no empty claim that only upon reaching the stage of Buddhahood do the general and the particular, the horizontal and the vertical, reach ultimate exhaustion.

Furthermore, as stated in the *Zhi guan* regarding the passage from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* on the initial arousal of the bodhicitta where both active and residual habits are exhausted, there is the teaching that [the Buddha] transcends the realm of the Muni within the world. However...

Regarding those who have passed beyond: since this encompasses both the fundamental afflictions (*mūlakleśa*) and the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), the "dust-like sands" of phenomena severed by the eight, nine, or ten stages of faith constitute the exhaustion of these habits.

It is not necessarily the case that "dust-like sands" themselves are the habitual tendencies. Furthermore, when the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* praises the virtues of Vimalakīrti as he dwells in the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), it states that he has no further residual habits.
The Great Master [Zhiyi] explained this with composure, asserting that although such [habits] exist...
It is as if non-existent; yet because there are subtle traces such as the stories of past words, it cannot be said to be entirely nothing.
One must still enter the gate of profound emptiness to break this habit; for when it is like non-existence and beyond words, there is no longer any salty flavor.
Thus, it cannot be said that they exist in their entirety, because they are as if non-existent. Therefore, it is said that there are no further residual habits (*vāsanā*).

This is how the two [statements] do not contradict one another. As for the ninth stage (*bhūmi*), the severing of the habitual tendencies of views and so forth—all of this is an exegesis that follows the scriptural text to clarify the meaning of the path of teaching.
Thus, the ignorance of the subsequent stages is taken as the residual habit. If this were not explained, then these textual passages would [otherwise remain unaccounted for].
Returning to the constant path, there are no more habitual tendencies to be severed. Therefore, what was previously called the forty-two stages of severance remains as it has always been;
if one’s faith accords with this teaching, that is precisely the meaning of "no more habitual tendencies."
Section on the Examples of Habitual Tendencies, Both General and Particular, and Their Similarities and Differences (25, 30, 31, 33, 34, 35, 44).
The Treatise states: Kāśyapa rose to dance upon hearing the lute, while Śāriputra recoiled from flowers out of fear of their form; these two cases share a commonality.
Regarding the discourse on the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the Mahāyāna, there are differences of preference and aversion;

these have already been examined in the *Miaozongchao* (as cited above), which may be considered exhaustive. Nevertheless, as there are still further points to be addressed, the Great Master synthesizes them into a single whole.
As stated in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-ṭīkā*: "Because residual afflictions have not yet been eliminated, one is defiled by the forms and sounds of the external realm;

therefore, it is rebuked by saying that since habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are not yet exhausted, flowers will cling to the body," as in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* regarding Kāśyapa hearing the lute and so forth.
Yet, Siming separated this into two parts, stating: "And so forth. This is why I have long been unable to resolve my doubts, until now...
It is for this reason that some have criticized [the Master]. Now, this treatise clarifies the matter therein. It says:

People of the time merely knew that the Four Clarities (Sīmānta) were divided into two, yet they did not realize that the Great Master also divided them. Does the text not say so? Therefore, the Heavenly Maiden rebuked him, saying:
"If within the Buddha-dharma there is one who makes distinctions, it is not in accordance with the Dharma. Since there are already distinctions, this is...

Regarding the entry into the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*): it is said that if the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) have not been exhausted, the flowers will adhere to the body; thus, there remain the delusions of thought (*bhāva-kleśa*) and so forth.
Therefore, one should know that within the Master’s own writings, both explanations are already included. Why, then, do you alone harbor doubts regarding Siming?

Speaking from this perspective, while Kāśyapa’s hearing of the lute was certainly of a single intent, Śāriputra’s fear of the flowers divided into two paths—namely, the path of attachment and the path of departure.
"Taking" refers to the meaning of attachment to the body; this is "discriminative thought," and discriminative thought is precisely ignorance (*avidyā*).

Therefore, in both instances in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, the phrase "flowers clinging to the body" is used to correspond to the afflictions of thought (*citta-kleśa*), as it indicates that the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) have not yet been exhausted.

If one takes the flowers away, this refers to "discriminative views"; discriminative views are precisely the "dust-like sands" [of secondary afflictions]. Thus, the *Miaozong* (The Sublime Commentary) extensively cites the passage from the *Vimalakīrti* that rebukes [the disciples for their inability to remove the flowers].
In this passage, the meaning of "fearing birth and death" is specifically taken up; thus, the "dust and sand" (countless afflictions) are pointed out as being merely habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
The reason for this is that, in contrast to the love for dancing, the flower is regarded as evil; it is because these two are categorized as dualistic delusions according to this specific pairing.
This is not unique to the Four Clarities (Sīmānanda); even the Great Master (Zhiyi) spoke thus.

For instance, he said that while the followers of the Two Vehicles (Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha) loathe the five desires (*pañca-kāma*) of the world and seek *nirvāṇa*, when they behold the retribution of the Bodhisattvas, they regard these five desires as improper;
yet though they abandon, reject, and push them away, they cannot depart from them. It continues until it says: "Heaven responds to this with a mind free of discrimination..."
While the mind of non-discrimination scatters [all distinctions], Śāriputra discriminates between saṃsāra and nirvāṇa as being different;

this is precisely what constitutes the delusion of views. Is this not consistent with his [the Buddha's] teaching? Nevertheless, this is spoken specifically from the perspective of the structural stages of the Dharma-gate.
Yet, it was not yet known that these possess a commonality; therefore, this treatise is further presented as a general discussion to perfect the explanation.

Herein, one should understand that although the two minds of attachment and aversion are divided into two distinct delusions and the two natures of grasping and rejecting, they fundamentally share a single mechanism.

From the outset, there are no two separate dharmas. Where there is attachment, there must be aversion; where there is both attachment and aversion, there are various mental perceptions (*manovijñāna*). These arise according to their respective objects, regardless of how they manifest.
This is because one who possesses the mind of Śāriputra rejecting the flower will dance upon encountering the lute of Kāśyapa;
yet one who possesses the mind of Kāśyapa rising to dance will recoil upon encountering Śāriputra’s flower and refuse its fruit. Fundamentally, they share a single mechanism.
The difference lies only in the terminology used. When arising from a mind of active attachment, it is called "volition" (*cetanā*);
when arising from discrimination and giving rise to craving, it is called "view" (*dṛṣṭi*). I fear that students might differentiate them based on these differences;
therefore, I have specifically established their commonality to ensure that the explanation is complete. One might ask: "Are sound and form also the same? I reply: "They are the same."

Regarding the superior and exquisite forms and sounds outside the realm, they are no different [from those within]. If they are indeed not different, why is there a distinction between the beautiful and the ugly?
To say "beautiful" and "ugly" does not refer to their superiority or inferiority. It is simply because, among the great objects of desire, none surpasses form;
therefore, one considers flowers to be contrary to the Dharma and strives to remove them. This is not said because they are base or inferior. Furthermore...
As Yuchi said: "Do not use such unlawful things. This [the suppression of color] is dull, yet the sound is sharp;

it is like a lute that, through its curved and ingenious construction, moves the heart and easily stirs the emotions. Does this not provide a profound analogy for the superior excellence of the Bodhisattva?
Thus, their likes and dislikes differ. However, Śāriputra merely removed the flower; by what means [could he have known otherwise]?
"Do you perceive the distinction between saṃsāra and nirvāṇa as a dualistic view? He replied, "It is by means of the subtle that one knows the manifest.
"When Cīraka heard the lute and rose to dance, it was appropriate for his primary retribution (*vipāka*). But why is it that even Mount Sumeru’s rising and falling does not bring peace?
He replied, "What kind of realm is this? To pose such a question regarding both the primary and secondary [retributions]. Nevertheless, there is indeed..."
Consider this carefully.
This text on demonstrating the severance of correct and habitual tendencies involves other related meanings and examples (1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 15, 29, 40, 43, 22).
The treatise says: Former scholars knew only to take their fixed interpretations as a means to challenge the text, yet they did not know how to take the text itself as the interpretation.

Now, if one takes fixed interpretations to challenge the text, then the text will invariably be obstructed; but if one takes the text itself as the interpretation, then there will be no principle that is not penetrated. Why is this?

For example, regarding the teaching of the Shared Vehicle (Tongjiao), which clarifies the doctrine of "retaining residual habits to moisten rebirth," some say: "To support the residual habits is to restrict them according to the [spiritual] stages."

There are distinctions based on cause and effect: either the cause is severed while the fruit remains, or the cause remains while the fruit is severed. If one were to insist upon a single interpretation, the text would become unintelligible;

therefore, each case follows its own specific meaning. However, when it is necessary to speak of "retaining the habit-energy" (*vāsanā*) for the sake of general consistency, it is because this teaching does not explain the transformation of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Upon reaching the fruition, there is no middle way, as it corresponds to the original state of an ordinary person.
Rebirth must necessarily arise from karma and afflictions (*kleśa*). If karma and afflictions were exhausted, one would ultimately return to extinction and annihilation;

such is the fundamental tenet of this teaching. Therefore, practicing alone cannot nourish rebirth; it requires the support of a vow (*praṇidhāna*) for rebirth to occur. A vow by itself also cannot draw forth rebirth;
it must accord with the fundamental tenets and rely upon practice for rebirth to occur. This is further termed "supporting practice" (*xi-fu*). This is why...

Regarding the claim that "the cause is severed while the fruit remains," this has never been a single, consistent position. Since the cause has already been severed, what fruit could possibly remain? By this, one knows that such a view is untenable.

As for the statement that one "proceeds from the contemplation of emptiness into the contemplation of the provisional, severing the ignorance of form and mind": *Note: The provided text contains a typographical error in the final phrase ("進" instead of "進斷"). The translation above reflects the intended meaning based on the context of the *Tiantai* doctrinal system.*
This refers to the demarcation of the stage of abandonment. In reality, however, benefiting sentient beings must necessarily involve intentionally retaining [afflictions] rather than abandoning them;
thus, upon reaching the stage of fruition, one still relies upon these residual habits (*vāsanā*) to manifest transformative activity.

This is precisely the meaning of the passage in the *Myōryaku* (Wondrous Joy) which, in demonstrating the stage of fruition, mentions that one may "retain residual habits from as far back as the seventh stage to moisten and sustain rebirth. If one were to abandon them at the causal stage while retaining them for the sake of fruition, then furthermore...
This is explained in terms of the predominance of cause and effect. Nevertheless, these are all arguments concerning the path of teaching (*śāsana-mārga*); the actual path (*bhūta-mārga*) is not so.

Furthermore, regarding the statement that Pratyekabuddhas eliminate residual habit-energies (*vāsanā*), there is no one who does not claim that they first eliminate the manifest [defilements] and subsequently eliminate the habits;

yet the Pratyekabuddha does not merely sever the manifest, but also eliminates the habit-energies. If this statement were true, then the *Xuanji* (Mysterious Record) would have already mentioned his "preemptive elimination" [of the habits].

To say it is not [the case] is incorrect (and so forth). Now I maintain that this too is a dogmatic interpretation that harms the text. One should first examine whether the traditional exegesis constitutes a definitive argument;
only then should one follow the text and adapt the explanation accordingly. For instance, regarding the traditional statement concerning "invasion" (*āśraya*) and "habituation" (*vāsanā*):

To what extent [does this apply]? Is it exhaustive or not? If it were exhaustive, how would it differ from a Bodhisattva? If it were not exhaustive, why would one call it the stage of a Pratyekabuddha?
The principle lies beyond mere habituation (*vāsanā*). Thus, we know that the text primarily demonstrates the relative depth and shallowness.

Therefore, as one follows the text to understand its shifts and transformations, one relies on the profound and correct [teaching] to approximate the penetration of habituation, thereby clarifying the shallow level of the Pratyekabuddha, while the commentary further contrasts it with the ultimate.
Speaking in terms of the fruit (*phala*) and the other shore (*pāra*), this already differs from the conventional approach.

Therefore, in the commentary, when explaining the text according to its literal sense, it specifically takes the "subduing" (*vibhava*) within the causal stage (*hetu*) to refer to "subduing. This means subduing the primary afflictions (*kleśa-mūla*);

as for the heavy ones, they do not arise, while the light ones are first eliminated so that subtle thoughts do not arise. This is why it is called "anticipatory incursion," yet it is not called "actual" (*samyak*).

The messenger [of the teaching] does not establish the fruits because they have not yet been regulated, and furthermore, because both [the afflictions and their seeds] are severed together. Speaking in terms of the two types of cultivation (*abhyāsa*), it is as when one says that the practice of a Pratyekabuddha does not establish the partial fruits;
this is merely to first indicate its underlying intent. If so, is it permissible for the preliminary cultivation (*pūrvābhyāsa*) to come before the correct [path]? One might say:
if we speak here in terms of "subduing and severing" (*vibhava-prahāṇa*), it does not lose its proper sequence. It is just like the Bodhisattvas of the Tripiṭaka, who first...

I have humbly examined your thoughts. Your point that "later one cuts off the *rajas* (dust-like afflictions)" is correct. Some might surely ask: "Upon reaching the fruit [of enlightenment], does one still further cut off the residual habits (*vāsanā*)?
This person, even during the causal stage, has already not produced even subtle thoughts; how much less so the residual habits thereafter?

Furthermore, it is clarified here that the penetration of these habits has no fixed limit; why then should one harbor doubts? Based on this, it is clear that the discourse regarding residual habits (*vāsanā*) is indeed not of a single path.

Furthermore, regarding the Samādhi of Profound Illumination and Immovability, there is the teaching that karma, as well as afflictions of view and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*), equally enter into conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and are thus objects to be destroyed.

Miaole (Zhili) indicates that there is regression at the six stages of mind; there is a fear that this refers to the passage stating that before this point, both view and thought afflictions are severed simultaneously.

These are all points of difficulty that have traditionally been raised in Japan. However, Siming already possesses established explanations on these matters... (and so forth). If one does not rely upon them...
It is commonly regarded as an obstacle; yet, if one takes the text itself as the basis for explanation, what further discussion could there be?

As for the meaning of the perfect severance (*pariccheda*), whether gradual or non-gradual, as elucidated by this school (the perfect severance being already clarified in the direct exposition), and regarding the various textual discrepancies and differing arguments—all of these can be understood by applying them analogously to similar categories.
Thus, no passage will pose a difficulty. If one merely follows a fixed interpretation and remains stubbornly attached to it...
"Grasp it! What shall I do? The *Yulun* (Discourse on Remainder) and the *Xialun* (Discourse on the Lower) state:
"Habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) originate from the fundamental afflictions (*anuśaya*); the fundamental afflictions begin with ignorance (*avidyā*). Thus, what is the cause of ignorance?"

As for its beginning, one must say it begins with ignorance (*avidyā*). It begins within the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena), yet the essence of *dharmatā* and ignorance are fundamentally non-dual;

thus, when one knows its beginning, that beginning is truly no beginning. If spoken of in relation to the myriad phenomena (*dharmas*), then the myriad phenomena begin with ignorance, rather than ignorance beginning with the myriad phenomena.
Therefore, it is said: "Ignorance is the beginning of delusion regarding the Truth."
Thus it is. Now, does ignorance have a beginning? Or is it without beginning? Or perhaps it has a beginning, yet one cannot know it? It is said:
This principle of "beginninglessness" has been discussed for a long time. For instance, the Dharma Master (Fuli) of the Tang dynasty once posed this as a verse to scholars throughout the land;
from ancient times, those who answered have not been uniform (as detailed in various records such as the *Zongjing*, *Jiaming*, *Linjian*, and *Ca'an* collections, etc.). Now...
I cannot spare the time to evaluate this in detail; for now, I shall directly present my explanation through two points. First, it is called "beginningless" because it is unknowable.
Second, it is called "beginningless" because its essence is fundamentally non-existent. What does this mean? Ignorance (*avidyā*) is the initial state of non-awakening.
Because of this non-awakening, emotion arises and wisdom becomes obstructed, like clouds covering the sky or dust settling on a mirror; thus, there must be a beginning to these conditions.
However, those who are deluded do not know this; this is the first meaning. If one ultimately transcends thought and severs the final limit, even then it cannot be known.
The subsequent aspect is like the initial one, and the initial aspect is like the subsequent one; their principle is non-dual.

Thus, although there is knowing, in reality it has no beginning and is ultimately unattainable. This is the second meaning. Furthermore, it does not depart from the principle of phenomena and reality.
Speaking in terms of principle (*li*), there is fundamentally no beginning and no end. Speaking in terms of phenomena (*shi*), there is a beginning and an end.

Because phenomena are themselves principle, although there is a beginning and an end, there is no beginning and no end. Because principle is itself phenomena, one speaks of a beginning and an end by way of that which has no beginning and no end.
Furthermore, it may be said that if the beginning and end reach their ultimate limit, they are no different from having neither beginning nor end.
These points are all the intended meaning of the texts in the *Awakening of Faith* and the commentaries on the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*; one can verify this by examining them. (And so forth.

I have also once responded with a verse, saying: "The vast and silent essence is empty; Silent illumination is neither arising nor non-arising. Since the place of arising has not yet fully manifested, What obstruction could prevent it from ceasing?"

Cease. This is like being weary at the onset of sleep; while dreaming, one seeks its beginning (the first meaning). One must have a person of great awakening to penetrate it—what principle could there be beyond this?
(the second meaning). It is not a matter of fearing that you do not know; rather, what is feared is the inability to die (and so forth).

Furthermore, if one speaks in terms of calculating by means of *xing* (nature), that which is beginningless is taken as having a beginning. If one speaks in terms of departing from *xing*, that which has a beginning is taken as beginningless. Although...
Even the present act of raising the mind or stirring a thought may be called "beginningless. This is as it is said:

"If one calculates based on self and other, claiming that they can give rise to all phenomena, then phenomena would have a beginning. Therefore, there is another verse that says: "Thought is the same as no-thought;

that which has no beginning is called the beginning. To know the start of the empty kalpa, realize it is fundamentally not separate from this very moment. Reflect upon this. Someone asked: "Regarding the Profound Text (Xuánwén)..."
Regarding the "Obstruction of Principle" (*zhànglǐ*) and the text of the *Xinyao* (Essentials of the Mind), how do they differ? It is said: they are not the same.

This is because the *Xuanyuan* (Profound Text) discusses only the Perfect [Teaching], and thus it addresses both the specific and general obstructions, such as ultimate emptiness and so forth. Since the meaning of the *Xinyao* is universal, when applied to the Perfect Teaching, it is the Perfect; when applied to the Separate Teaching, it is the Separate.
If one is partial, one remains partial. Yet, apart from the specific [afflictions of] views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), why is fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*) further mentioned? It is said:

this is merely a difference in terminology regarding whether it is associated or independent. However, once the general and specific aspects of views and thoughts have been fully exhausted, [the discussion is complete].

How can there be what is called a "directly obstructing delusion regarding principle"? It is said: Although this may be so on the surface, it cannot be considered entirely distinct [from other categories].

It is merely that the terminology from which they are derived differs; it does not mean their essence is separate. For example, retributive wisdom (*vipākajñāna*) is one and the same, yet it is described as "conforming above to the profound" and "harmonizing below with the mundane," and so forth.
Someone asked: Among the myriad texts, some divide [delusions] into three grades, while others speak of those within the realms (*dhātu*).

Externally, combining two with three results in a discrepancy that does not correspond; one might also inquire whether they can be reconciled. [The Master] said: "This also follows the teachings, and its expansion or contraction is not fixed.
For example, in the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*), because it only severs what is within the realm, it does not distinguish between grades.

Since this teaching encompasses both the internal and external realms, and because the stages of the *rajas-aṇu* (dust-motes) are long, the ten abodes (*daśabhūmi*) pertain to the internal realm. Since these constitute the lower grade, then the meanings of the middle and upper grades [apply to the external]."

When one is outside the realm, it becomes clear. By analogy, the same should apply to the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*) in the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*); it is simply that the duration of these stages is so brief that they are not differentiated. Someone may ask:

"If the 'dust-sands' [of phenomena] do not moisten birth, why does the text say, 'If there were no dust-sands of skillful means (*upāya*), then birth would not occur,' and further state, 'Immeasurable dust-sands bring about immeasurable retributions'?
What is the meaning of this? The answer is: The Master of the Commentary (*Jizhu*) has already resolved this himself.
The text states: "Dust and sand do not truly moisten those born outside the realms; their drawing forth of retribution is entirely due to non-outflow karma (*anāsrava-karman*) as the cause.
Non-outflow karma refers to the mind that clings to emptiness. Because it clings to emptiness, it fails to comprehend all phenomena (*dharma*).

Taking these incomprehended phenomena as a point of reference, they are provisionally opposed to the lands, and thus dust and sand may also be used to represent them; this refers to the first passage cited above.
The subsequent text also establishes that each of the three delusions possesses the intent to summon and accumulate karmic retribution;

thus, by means of other capacities, the "dust and sand" afflictions refer to *darśana-heya* (delusions abandoned through insight) and *bhāvanā-heya* (delusions abandoned through cultivation), which indeed carry the meaning of summoning retribution. All of this is merely a general statement. Someone may ask:

The *Miaozong* states that the layers of *darśana-heya* and *bhāvanā-heya* are like dust or sand. To what specific category among these "dust and sand" *darśana-heya* and *bhāvanā-heya* does this refer?

The delusion is called "dust-sand" (resembling the sands of the Ganges). As for what is called the "multiple layers of view-delusion and thought-delusion," this refers to those very view- and thought-delusions which are the ailments known through the Bodhisattva’s provisional contemplation (*jia-guan*).

It simply means that there are as many such layers as exist; furthermore, when one recognizes both the medicines and so forth, this constitutes provisional contemplation, whereas not knowing them constitutes dust-sand.
Therefore it is said: "Dust-sand is not itself an obstruction; rather, it is the obstruction that obstructs dust-sand."

This is precisely its meaning. Someone asked: "Where are the dust-like afflictions of the two vehicles severed? If they are not severed, how can they come in the future to teach and transform sentient beings?
I replied: "There are indeed specific times and places. For example, when the Prajñāpāramitā bestows its empowerment upon the two individuals, they turn the teaching and take up their karmic duties."
The speaker and the listener—this is precisely the meaning. It should break through the sands of dust (asamkhyeya-dharmas), as stated in the text at length. Someone may ask:

"The sands of dust severed during the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*) in the Perfect Teaching should encompass both the internal and external; why then is it said that at the moment of first generating the mind of enlightenment, both the active and habitual tendencies are exhausted?"

This refers simply to the exhaustion of the correct practice within the realm [of the ten abidings]. It is said that if one considers the vertical severance of the three delusions, these *rajas* (dust-like) delusions would be exhausted by the end of the Ten Faiths;
however, because these *rajas* delusions now extend through to the subsequent stages, they are distinguished as "internal" or "external" in relation to the True and the Simulated.

Someone may ask: Regarding what Four Ming calls the "habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*)—the exhaustion of both common and distinct habitual tendencies—the principle of this explanation is indeed comprehensive. Yet, does it not also...?

"Is there scriptural evidence for this? He replied, "It is not that there is no textual basis. As clarified above, the eighth, ninth, and tenth stages of faith (śraddhā) exhaustively sever the residual habits (*vāsanā*) within the realm of conditioned existence (*dhātu*).

Yet, the *Fǔxíng* (Subcommentary on the *Mohe Zhiguan*) states: 'Residual habits extend beyond the realm [of conditioned existence], including the dust-like ignorance (*rajas-tulya-avidyā*) and the ignorance of the unconditioned (*anabhilāpya-avidyā*).

Is it not the case, therefore, that the dust-like ignorance also extends to the subsequent stages? Furthermore, as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: 'Even Bodhisattvas of the ten stages still possess residual habits, because regarding all phenomena, they..."*
Because there is that which is not yet known. Is this not precisely pointing to the fact that the "dust-like sands" [of phenomena] pervade all ten stages?

Yet, if the dust-like sands have already been severed at the stage of the Ten Faiths, how could there be anything remaining unknown upon reaching this [stage]? [The answer is: The statement regarding "not knowing" does not refer merely to what is learned through study;

it correctly indicates that because one's position has not yet reached ultimate consummation, both principle (*li*) and phenomena (*shi*) have not yet been fully manifested. Only then will one understand what was said previously. Its...
The meaning accords with this. Someone asked: "The text regarding 'unexhausted habitual tendencies' (vāsanā) originally derives from the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*;

why then does the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* point out that it is taught as 'habitual tendencies' in the Śrāvaka sūtras? Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* and the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* clarify two kinds of ignorance which originally derive from the Hīnayāna;
why then do they state that 'dust-like sands' (*rajovāluka*) are themselves habitual tendencies? He replied: "Pure..."
The text of this [treatise] is titled [the *Ming-mo lun*]. Although it is not of the Hīnayāna, it nonetheless speaks by concealing its true intent when addressed to those of the Two Vehicles;

thus, in meaning, it corresponds to the Śrāvaka sūtras, though it does not mean that it belongs to the Lesser Teaching (*hīnayāna*). As for the text of the second treatise, it likely summarizes the general purport of the teachings and is not primarily concerned with the fundamental [Mahāyāna] doctrine;
because it was spoken for the sake of those of the Two Vehicles, it is permissible to speak of it in such a way. Someone may ask: "In the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*, why were the flowers removed?"

Regarding the text on the habit-energies (*vāsanā*) of the fetters: [the fetters] such as those of Kāśyapa and others were originally distinct fetters; how can they be pointed to as the habit-energies of the universal fetters? Answer:
To speak according to reality, although these are specific delusions, for the sake of the Two Vehicles (*dviyāna*), it may be said that they are indeed the universal habit-energies.

Someone asked: In the *Xuánjì* (Profound Record) on Guanyin, while explaining the thirty-four moments of mind where both the primary afflictions and their habit-energies are exhausted, there is a statement that says: "In one word..."

Regarding "habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*): there are the habitual tendencies of views and afflictions (*kleśa*), as well as the habitual tendencies of the *dharmas* as numerous as motes of dust (*rajas*), and so forth. However, this single passage is questionable for three reasons.

First, it is doubtful because, according to the common tradition, one should simply say these are the "primary and habitual tendencies of views and afflictions"; yet here, the *rajas* [tendencies] are included in the explanation.

Second, it is doubtful because if one follows what is severed by Bodhisattvas—namely, that in order to transform sentient beings they originally first sever the *rajas* [tendencies]—then the present mention of the two types of tendencies occurring simultaneously would be inconsistent. Third, it is doubtful because... [text fragment].
[The text] ends there; this is the second point of doubt. Generally speaking, the "dust-and-sand" dharma-gates and the Four Noble Truths are fundamentally distinct;

yet here they are spoken of together—this is the third point of doubt. Now, I shall explain them in sequence: according to the standard interpretation found in various texts, when reaching the fruit [of Buddhahood], one speaks only of severing the "correct" and "habitual" aspects of *darśana-heya* (afflictions to be abandoned by insight) and *bhāvanā-heya* (afflictions to be abandoned by cultivation).
This is precisely because the "dust-and-sand" afflictions have already been exhausted beforehand. However, in this present text...
It is also said: "The Bodhisattva cultivates and studies the *dharmamukhas* as numerous as dust motes and sand grains to remedy inferior wisdom; is this not the prior severance?

Yet it is said that [afflictions and knowledge] are exhausted simultaneously. This is because when the *dharmas* as numerous as dust motes and sand grains are spoken of in conjunction with the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), it reveals that the two truths are simultaneous, thereby fully manifesting the state of fruition.
This is also the specific teaching of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*), wherein both the active afflictions (*vāsana*) and the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) are exhausted, reaching the ultimate.
This accords with the Buddha’s intention; therefore, one should know that whatever meanings the Four Clarifications (Sì míng) explains are certainly not in vain.
Otherwise, why would it differ from other texts? Let students further examine this in detail.
The General Preface to the Fifth Treatise on Contemplating Dharmas, Part One, states:
In clarifying principle, nothing takes precedence over the teachings; in realizing the Way, nothing is closer than the gates of contemplation. Without the teachings, there is no principle...

There is no way to manifest it. If one abandons contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), by what means could the Way be realized? Therefore, the fundamental tenets of this school truly take these two as the ferry for entering the Way.
For teaching has the function of elucidating through expression, which necessarily relies upon verbal discourse;

whereas contemplation has the essence of realization through awakening, which lies in the forgetting of words. Yet, without words, there would be no way to manifest the ultimate state of wordlessness; and without wordlessness, [the ultimate cannot be reached].
Without this, one cannot penetrate the subtlety of verbal expression. Thus, if one realizes according to the teaching, then the teaching itself transcends words;

yet if one cultivates according to what has been heard, then contemplation likewise involves speech. For now, let us set aside the teachings and discuss contemplation. As for contemplation, it began in the Northern Qi dynasty.

The *Zhonglun* (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā) was obtained from within these [teachings] in four lines. The method of contemplating phenomena (*dharmas*) originated with Nāgārjuna, who transmitted it to Huiyuan of Mount Nan;
Huiyuan, in turn, bestowed it upon Zhiyi of Tiantai. At that time, this method of contemplation was both extremely simple and essential.

The transmission between master and disciple may truly be called solemn. There were many who grasped its essence and attained intuitive realization through silent resonance. It was only because he [Zhiyi] adapted outwardly to the times...
It is appropriate to harmonize this with the sūtras and śāstras, supplementing it with the teachings of the present age.

Yet, among those who advance in their cultivation, some fail to find the gateway, while others encounter obstructions. Seeing that the varieties of ailments and medicines are manifold and that hindrances are not uniform, one must further broaden the path of the vehicles and their objects;
for every contemplation and every practice, there is a corresponding method. Thus, through these religious teachings and contemplations, one proceeds with ease.
All these were fully prepared. As for those who brought great clarity to the era, their tradition dates back to ancient times.
Nevertheless, the school of the Four Phrases and Three Contemplations also grew increasingly extensive and widespread, such that there were many instances where the original source was lost.

This was not because they did not know how to maintain this Way to solemnize its transmission; rather, it was simply because at times there were unavoidable circumstances. Yet, they still successively followed one another’s teachings and honored the lineage.
I have received [this teaching], which traces back to the very source and origin and was transmitted to the ultimate point at Siming.

From that time on, the school split into branches and lineages, and divergent theories arose in profusion. Biased views and distorted studies muddied its midst, resulting in such a chaotic proliferation that it is impossible to record them all.
Down to the present day, this decline has become unbearable; thus, the Way of observing the Dharma has daily decayed, and the doctrines of its lineage have increasingly fallen into affliction.
Even when there are occasional proponents who speak of it, they mostly fail to grasp its essential meaning.

Since their judgments are frequently misplaced and incorrect, how could I venture to place my trust in them at such a hasty moment? This is why this treatise cannot be dispensed with. Nevertheless, while there are many gates to observation, practice likewise is not...

First: Thus, taking the "three thousand realms in a single thought-moment" as the fundamental substance of the contemplative method, and the three types of contemplation as the pivotal mechanism for teaching and practice, the distinctions between the ten vehicles and four practices, as well as the differences between phenomena and principle, or teaching and contemplation, are so manifold that they cannot be fully exhausted in a single approach.
Here, I shall briefly cite several examples to illustrate them, so that the principles of this simple and easy path may be clearly observed.
Furthermore,
in the separate examples to the right,
the texts concerning the methods of contemplation (*guanfa*) total sixty-five. Of these, nine state the general principles of the three thousand [realms], while three...
There are ten categories of contemplative methods (*guanfa*). Regarding the "contemplative characteristics of the ten vehicles" (*shicheng guanshang*), there are two.

Regarding the "four kinds of samādhis," there are seven. Regarding the "two contemplations of phenomena and principle" (*shili erguan*), there are eight. Regarding the "contemplation that initiates the teaching and applies to what is cultivated by beginners," there is one.

Regarding the "contemplation of the mind and the contemplation of the Buddha," there is one. Regarding the "three superior and distinct contemplations that encompass other contemplative characteristics," there are three. Regarding the "universal... [the text ends].

There are seventeen instances concerning the three contemplations of marks (*lakṣaṇa-tri-vipaśyanā*); seven instances clarifying the non-duality of object and contemplation along with supplementary meanings; totaling ten categories.
Regarding the general principles of the Three Thousand [Great Meanings], these correspond to sections sixteen, eighteen, nineteen, twenty, twenty-one, twenty-six, thirty-six, and forty-one.
(43) The Treatise says:
Now, "Three Thousand" is the collective name for all phenomena (*dharmas*) and a distinctive designation for their perfect completion.
Our Buddha took this as the realm of realization; the *Lotus Sūtra* took this as the grand outline of its revelation; and Tiantai took this as...

This is the Dharma-gate of practice, which takes cessation and contemplation as its guiding compass. Thus, when speaking of its phenomena, there is no realm or worldly thing that it does not encompass;
yet when tracing its principle back to its source, there is no subtle nature among the Three Truths that it does not manifest.
To demonstrate its literary expression, it originates from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*; to establish its discourse, its merit is attributed to Zhiyi.
Were it not for the Perfect Mind (*yuanxin*), nothing could encompass it; were one to set aside wondrous awakening, who could clarify it?

To harmonize the myriad phenomena and return them to the One Mind, and to realize the Three Truths through that very One Mind—this can only be the "Three Thousand" (*sanqian*). Indeed, the principle of these Three Thousand is profoundly sublime.
Profound indeed! If one attains its source and foundation, it becomes self-evident. Now, I shall briefly discuss it through four meanings:

first, that the original intent lies solely in the contemplation of the inherent; second, that the three truths are what is manifested therein; third, that phenomena and principle are fundamentally of one essence.

The fourth point is as follows: it consists of possessing no divergent paths. Once these four intentions are attained, more than half of the essential principles of the Three Thousand Worlds have been contemplated.
Furthermore, one will not be muddied by heterodox arguments. What is meant by "the fundamental intention is solely the contemplation of the inherent presence"?

This refers to the contemplative path of our school, which discusses all phenomena through the Perfect Teaching; it must take the single nature as its foundation. The subtlety of this single nature is such that the three truths are naturally present. This is the Mahā... [text ends]

Regarding *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, the inconceivable realm, and the reason for clarifying the hundred realms and thousand suchnesses (*sahasra-tathatā*)—that the three thousand worlds reside within a single thought-moment without priority or sequence—is because the essential principle (*zong*) lies in the completeness of contemplation (*guan*).
Thus it is called "the contemplative gate of this one school" (*yijia guanmen*), precisely because contemplation is complete, and so forth.

As Chen Liaoweng’s *Verses on the Gate of the Three Thousand Possessions* further captures this meaning: "If there were even a single dharma that existed apart from the mind, [it could not be attained]."
If [the teaching] arose from [a mere] nature, then phenomena would become partial and deviant, for their essence would not be eternally abiding.
Thus, taking the wondrousness of the three thousand [realms] as a guide for the contemplation of dharmas—to finally reach the ultimate and most profound exposition—is truly for a good reason.

Therefore, one should know that without clarifying the three thousand, there is no way to demonstrate the inherent inclusion of nature; without clarifying the three thousand, there is no way to realize "mind-only"; without clarifying the three thousand...
To penetrate the subtlety of the Dharma, one cannot do so without clarifying the three thousand realms; without clarifying the three thousand realms, there is no way to know that the essence is one;

without clarifying the three thousand realms, there is no way to manifest the fusion of nature; without clarifying the three thousand realms, there is no way to perceive the dimensions of the essence; and without clarifying the three thousand realms, there is no way to reveal the virtues of fruition.
Without clarifying the three thousand [realms], there is no means to recognize the perfect mind; without clarifying the three thousand, there is no means to distinguish it from the partial vehicles;
without clarifying the three thousand, there is no means to manifest the fundamental tenet. Thus, the teaching of the three thousand manifests itself in this manner.

How could those of the past have regarded the three thousand as being fixedly illusory or provisional, as not being the Way, as merely differential phenomena, or as things produced by causes and conditions?
To claim that because of ignorance there is this delusion which must be destroyed—how extremely perverse is this, contradicting both the ancestors and the fundamental tenets!
Even if there were one or two textual passages or meanings to rely upon, each would necessarily have its own specific intent; how could one fail to investigate the reasons behind them?
Yet you simply treat them as delusive assertions. The meaning of those texts shall be understood later. What is meant by "the three truths are that which is manifested"? Truly...
Although the characteristics of phenomena are vast and the number of phenomena is great, when their essential substance is examined, they do not transcend the Three Truths;

yet it is precisely through the Three Truths that the Three Thousand Worlds come to exist. Thus, they are not non-existent, for it is by virtue of emptiness (*śūnyatā*)—as the pervasive characteristic—that they arise.

It is through the Provisional that the three thousand [realms] are manifested; it is not that they are absent in the Provisional. Because manifestation occurs by means of the Provisional, one is able to manifest the three thousand.
It is not that they are absent in the Middle; because integration and inclusion occur by means of the Middle, one is able to include the three thousand.
Thus, each of the Three Truths fulfills its respective meaning to constitute the three thousand. Otherwise, the dharma of the three thousand would not even be able to exist.
How much more so, then, could one exhaust its subtlety? Thus, the three thousand realms are not three thousand realms; their essence is the Three Truths. The Three Truths are not three truths;
they do not depart from the single nature. Therefore, when observing the Three Truths from the perspective of this single nature, the Three Truths are not three.
Furthermore, by means of the three truths, the three thousand [realms] are revealed; thus, the three thousand are fundamentally one.
Because the three thousand are fundamentally one, they are numbers yet not numbers. Because the three truths are not three, they are names yet not names.

Since they are names yet not names and numbers yet not numbers, the single nature that is revealed is neither fixedly empty, provisional, nor middle, yet it is never separate from emptiness, provisionality, and the middle. Thus, it is said to exist.
Marks and the absence of marks have never, from the very beginning, existed as either being or non-being; therefore, it is said that there is only the single true nature (*ekasatya-dharmatā*).
It is further said that the three truths (*trisatya*) are formless and all are invisible;

this is precisely the principle revealed by the three truths. Thus, when taken as the object (*ālambana*), that object is wondrous; when taken as the contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), that contemplation is harmonious; and when used to manifest the nature, that nature is...

It is manifested through this that one accomplishes virtue. When virtue is complete, it reaches the point where one says: "Thus, the provisional dharma may be used to clarify matters through events," and so forth;
this, however, merely employs names and words to distinguish characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). It is not what is meant by manifesting the essential nature (*tattva*).

Now, when one employs names and words to distinguish characteristics, there must necessarily be the sense of formal opposition and so on; therefore, in the case of names and characteristics, they cannot be [the ultimate reality].

This is not so. Furthermore, how could this possibly constitute a definitive doctrine? Yet some, failing to understand and failing to investigate what is revealed, do not grasp the underlying principle.

They instead compete over the names and characteristics of that which reveals, engaging in debates regarding "having characteristics" versus "being without characteristics," and consequently explain the Three Truths as being mutually exclusive.
Moreover, they restrict the "three thousand realms" to the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) alone. To establish a school based on such views is certainly not correct.

Their differences lie herein. Yet even those who support our school have not yet attained correctness; for all fail to take the root source as their foundation and instead merely occupy themselves with the trivialities of names and appearances.
It is clear that they are insufficient to be consulted regarding this Way. What is meant by "phenomena and principle being fundamentally one body"?
Regarding the meaning of phenomena and principle, it is certainly not a single path; however, when speaking in terms of the Three Thousand [Realms], phenomena and principle do not exceed these.

The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) says: "First, regarding the principle (*li*), etc. What is called "creation by principle" refers to the inherent nature (*xingju*). "Creation by phenomena" (*shizao*) refers to that which is produced through conditions, namely the phenomena of the ten realms.

However, the principle has no fixed location; it is omnipresent within phenomena. This is truly because the principle is inherently present (*lijù*) that there can subsequently be the functional activity of phenomena.
Thus, where there is no principle, there are no phenomena; and where there are no phenomena, there is no principle. There is no foundation other than the fusion of principle and phenomena.
Matters (phenomena) encompass principle through these matters; thus, this perfect and sudden teaching holds that their source is one and their essence is non-dual.

Therefore it is said: "Perfectly seeing matters and principle, they are fully present in a single thought-moment. To take up even a single dharma, both matter and principle are therein complete. It is simply the three thousand [realms];
whether one follows matter or follows principle, two meanings are provisionally distinguished. Thus, when speaking from the perspective of inherent possession, it is the three thousand.

This is "creation by principle. Speaking in terms of its own transformation, the three thousand [realms] are "creation by phenomena. Although phenomenon and principle differ, they are fundamentally one and the same in essence.

Furthermore, although two meanings are manifested, it is precisely to reveal the virtues of the nature (*dharmatā*). If one knows that within phenomena the three thousand are entirely created by principle, it not only reveals the nature, but the virtues possessed therein are also revealed;
for there is nothing created that is not the mind-nature. Now, by means of this...

The three thousandfold aspects of phenomena and principle are both manifested herein; this is truly the case. Since this is so for phenomena and principle, it is likewise true for cultivation and nature, essence and function.
As it is said: "The clarity of the mirror is the ten realms of nature; the arising of images is the ten realms of cultivation. Thus, form and image represent cultivation and nature.

The inner and outer of the mirror are one. Furthermore, it is said: "The three thousand realms are all eternally present; both essence and function are identical. These are all its essential points. (And so forth.

Yet some generally equate emptiness with the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) as being "phenomenon" (*shi*) and "principle" (*ri*), and further claim that the essence of principle is definitively without distinction, while the function of phenomena is definitively possessed of distinction.
They even say: "Do not speak with deceptive confusion on the grounds that they are mutually identical."
Now, I say: while it is true that such distinctions exist within the textual gateways of provisional analysis, to hold them as definitive doctrine is to err.

This would be partial and restrictive, utterly contradicting the essence of the Dharma; such distorted discourse cannot even be maintained without internal inconsistency, so how could it possibly be correct?
What is meant by "identity" (*ji*) and "endowment" (*ju*) being without difference? Indeed, the discussion of identity and endowment originated with our own school, and it must necessarily...

This is indeed clear and illuminating; it is finally the attainment of the essential meaning. Why? For instance, in the *Zhi guan*, it is clarified that a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*) is endowed with the three thousand realms.

Furthermore, it says: "The three thousand realms are precisely this one thought-moment; this one thought-moment is precisely the three thousand realms. They are neither prior nor posterior. This is the greatest expression of "simultaneous inclusion" (*yiqie yu*).

One must still understand this: that which is "suchness" (ji) cannot lack "provisional manifestation" (ju), and provisional manifestation cannot lack suchness. If there were suchness without provisional manifestation, it would not be perfect suchness;
if there were provisional manifestation without suchness, it would not be sudden provisionality. When there is sudden provisionality, there is no phenomenon that is not suchness;

when there is perfect suchness, there is no phenomenon that is not provisionally manifested. If suchness and provisionality were each explained in isolation without mutually constituting and revealing one another, then even the preceding partial teachings could be so described.
Only when one possesses both "immediacy" (*ji*) and "endowment" (*ju*) can it be called "perfectly comprehensive" (*yuan-quan*).

Therefore, it is said to be "immediate" and "endowed. This refers specifically to the stages of the Perfect and the Distinct Teachings. Thus, when speaking of "immediacy," it is in terms of endowment; when speaking of "endowment," it is in terms of immediacy.

Because one speaks of immediacy precisely through endowment, although there are the three thousand dharmas of the inherent nature (*xing-de*), they do not merely possess the nature; they are also immediate within phenomena (*shi*).

This is the nature of phenomena (*lakṣaṇa*). Because one discusses the inclusion [of all phenomena] precisely through their essential unity, although one cultivates the three thousand [realms] within the principle of nature (*li-xing*), this does not hinder the vivid manifestation of all various characteristics.
Thus, it is simply these same three thousand [realms] that are discussed in terms of both cultivation and nature; it is simply these same three thousand [realms].

The treatise already contains this; there is no divergence in principle. Yet some claim that while the three thousand [dharmas] are complete in principle, they are complete as nature (*xing*) but not complete as phenomena (*xiang*);
at the moment of "identity" (*ji*), not a single dharma exists. Furthermore, they say that in "identity," it is the phenomenon (*shi*) that acts as the agent of identity.
"Principle (li) is that which is identical [to phenomena]; to say it possesses [phenomena] is the opposite of this. (And so forth. Now I say:

That explanation may be granted as a provisional view, for it attains the sense of a formal contrast with partiality and strength. However, in the second sense, it is not so. How could the principle of the Perfect and Sudden identity-and-possession (yuan-dun ji-jù) be clarified through such limited and biased attachments?
Nevertheless, the doctrine of Xiachuan is indeed as you have refuted it; whether it is correct or not can thus be known. And yet—
Why has the essential tenet of Siming never been explicitly stated? It is said that Siming has no distinct tenet other than the very capacity to clarify [the truth].
Thus, the tenet of Siming is precisely the tenet of Jingxi and Tiantai.
By simply taking the textual meanings from both sides and synthesizing them through interpretation, there is nothing that does not harmonize; therefore, it was not set forth separately.
It is the inconceivable provisional [nature], not the partial provisional. This basis of the provisional possesses all dharmas.
It is true emptiness that is not empty; it is not merely empty. It is perfect centrality that is perfectly fulfilled; it is not merely central.

Therefore, the first of the four gates (originally three) is precisely this inconceivable provisional nature. The first gate is the three, and the three are the one. (Omitting one phrase) It is like the four fingers.
(The original text numbers 1, 2, 3, and 4) point to a single moon. Although the four dots appear distinct, they are but a single gate of emptiness (*śūnyatā-dvāra*).

Each and every gate is the *dharmadhātu*. (Omitted line). If one does not contemplate through the gate of wondrous provisional existence, who would know that the *dharmadhātu* is fully endowed with all phenomena?
Through hearing, reflection, cultivation, and realization, there is no mind that is not wondrous, for it is able to contemplate this essence as being complete. If one contemplates only the mind...
Regarding the "contemplation of inclusion," one contemplation is divided into two schools. One school holds that the gate of contemplation differs from various other doctrines;
yet while these doctrines differ from one another, the contemplation itself remains one. Those [of the former school] are deluded regarding the fact that the one mind includes all phenomena;

they fall into the categories of the general and the particular, and within the sequential, they further posit a sequence, thereby giving rise to the notion of sequential severance. How could they know that the ten realms are fundamentally the eternal one, and that the three thousand [realms] are fundamentally one?
It is also thus. None of these can be distinguished by worldly categories. (The following eight phrases are omitted as their meaning seems unsettled.
Within the wondrous realm—which is originally neither empty, provisional, nor middle—it is nonetheless not separate from emptiness, the provisional, and the middle. Emptiness is itself the mind.
(Originally composed as emptiness) Provisionally, this is form. (Originally composed as mind) It is neither form nor mind; it is called the "Middle. It is where form and mind are transcended;
there, the reality of the Middle manifests. This is present in the essence of each and every phenomenon. When the ordinary person’s mind is complete, it is the Buddha’s completeness.
If one grasps and clings, it is not complete. The single word "complete" (*ju*) reveals the present school. Those who enter this school are most... (originally composed as...)

10) Rare and Wondrous (The following are Chen Liaoweng’s verses on the “Three Thousand Existences,” now appended here with slight revisions and the occasional alteration of one or two characters, so as to preserve their essential significance).
In the examples from the *Sanlun lun* (with the "Union of Schools" appended), the treatise states:
"Those who clarify the great purport certainly master the meaning of the text; those who are obscure regarding the meaning of the text have necessarily not yet mastered the great purport."

Therefore, following the general outline, I shall now discuss the meaning of the textual passages. However, while the texts concerning the "three thousand" are numerous, those appearing in this specific category number only nine.
Now, I shall summarize and discuss them, comparing them with other texts to distinguish their similarities and differences; there are five general categories.

First, a discussion on the source of the three thousand: according to the indications in the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary), the "three thousand in a single thought-moment" (*yīniàn sānqiān*) refers exclusively to the [contemplation of] cessation (*śamatha*).

[The author] regards this as the ultimate and most profound teaching, something never before mentioned in other texts. However, while the text produced is but one, there are three ways it is applied. First, regarding the distinction between the partial (pian) and the perfect (yuan):

it is taught that [the three thousand realms] exist only within the perfect and the distinct (bie), but not in the [partial] teachings. As clarified in the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary on the *Mohe Zhiguan*), it states that ordinary beings possess the three thousand realms within their minds.
Regarding this, some say: "Since the Distinct Teaching breaks down the nine [realms] to reveal the one, the realms gradually decrease; thus, it is not said [that they exist in the partial]."
The Three Thousand [Realms] are clear. How is it that the *Commentary on the Treatise on Contemplating the Mind* says such-and-such? Is this not another instance of "explaining"? I say: not so.
For example, the *Commentary and Record on the Vimalakīrti Sūtra* states: "If ordinary persons possess the Three Thousand within delusion, can this also be called 'explaining'?
Therefore, for this reason, it is said: to speak of ordinary persons possessing the Three Thousand is to say that ordinary persons are deluded.

The "Middle" [teaching] explains the three thousand [dharmas], yet one cannot thereby categorically equate this with the distinct teaching (*biejiao*) which asserts that the essence itself possesses the three thousand. Thus, it may be said that the distinct teaching speaks of the three thousand;

however, it must be understood that this [explanation] cannot be used to dismantle [the Middle teaching]. Nevertheless, regarding the text of the *Guānxīn lùn shū* (Commentary on the Treatise on Contemplating the Mind), how is it that it clearly states this?
One might say: although that text appears to speak of the three thousand, it does not [assert them] as being identical to the mind.

It is complete. Furthermore, it says: "This Tathāgatagarbha is fully endowed with [all qualities]," and so forth. Thus we know that this pertains to the fruition and not the cause; it still belongs to the meaning of the path of teaching (*śāsana-mārga*).
Moreover, there is no fault in explaining the text according to the post-nirvāṇa period. Second, regarding the distinction between the former and the present:

the Perfect [Teaching] of the past cannot be spoken, whereas the Perfect [Teaching] of the present can be spoken, because in the past the two vehicles were not yet opened up to reveal their attainment of Buddhahood. Thus, the principle of the Three Thousand [Worlds]... [is established].
It is deficient. Only the present sutra [the Lotus Sūtra] opens up the provisional to reveal the real; as a single path, it is without partiality.

Therefore, it is said that the "pointing to" the wondrous realm originates from the *Lotus Sūtra*, namely the passage on the "ten suchnesses. Now, if the ten suchnesses are simply the phenomena of cause and effect, how could there be anything to be "pointed to"?
Some argue this based on the *Golden Needle*, claiming that the ten suchnesses must necessarily encompass the ten realms and so forth. I, however, say that this is not necessarily so.
However, one should specifically point to the single phrase "the beginning and the end are ultimately equal" (*benmo jiujing deng*); this alone is what emerges from the wondrous realm (and so forth).

Third, regarding the three divisions (*sanbu*), this refers to the teachings of *Zhiguan* (Stopping and Contemplation), whereas the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning) does not mention them. Herein lies both a general and a specific sense. Generally speaking, the "realms" (*jie*) and "suchness" (*ru*) are none other than the three thousand [realms].
Thus, one should know that the *Xuanyi* could also have spoken of them; it is merely that the paths of teaching and contemplation differ, and thus the three thousand...
Regarding the purport of these [teachings], whether they are required or not, there are thus variations in their detail and brevity. As for the two treatises and the two commentaries upon them:
if the definitive, wondrous realm originates from the *Lotus Sūtra*, how can one instead use the two commentaries to explain the text of the *Avataṃsaka*?

It is said that each text has its own purpose, and their essential meaning is established through the True Aspect (*dharmatā*). Why is this? Since the "Ten Suchnesses" are presented in relation to the revelation and manifestation [of the Buddha-nature], they are described as being ultimately equal.
Thus, there is no dharma that is not wondrous. Therefore, it is said that the wondrous realm originates from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

Since "mind-creation" (*cittakṛta*) encompasses both the meanings of phenomena and principle, one may cite "creation" as proof for "endowment. It is therefore appropriate to explain the text of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* by means of these two types of creation.

As for their mutual establishment, the wondrous realm of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is not devoid of the principle of the two creations; how could the "mind-creation" of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* be incompatible with the wondrous realm?

...this discussion. However, as the intent of the specific section is not convenient [for this context], I have followed an alternative interpretation for now; these points are all shown as in the separate [text]. (etc.

Regarding whether the Three Treatises involve attachment or not: if, according to the *Zhi guan*, one does not possess the three thousand realms due to a mind of attachment, yet the *Fuxing* also states that there are those among the practitioners of the Perfect Teaching who do not know the mutual pervasiveness—what is the meaning of this? It is said: if we discuss the state of being without-mind...

It is already so. Being present for even a moment, it is fully complete. How could there be attachment such that it would not be complete? However, regarding this statement, one must understand two meanings:

first, a comprehensive inclusion based on its essence; second, an exclusion based on the state of the mind. Speaking according to the first meaning, since there is not even "no-mind" to be excluded, how could there be a "mind" that is not complete?
Speaking according to the second meaning, everything from the path of the Distinct Teaching (biejiao) downward is included therein.
This is the case even for the examples being excluded; how much more so for grasping at deluded thoughts?

Nevertheless, if one realizes that deluded thoughts possess not a single distinct characteristic, then the three thousand [realms] are complete right where they are, without needing to seek them afar.

As for the subsequent text, it merely uses the inability to grasp the meaning as a means to demonstrate universal completeness. Therefore, it says: "If one follows ordinary sentiments and gives rise to views of internal and external, then even though it is perfect..."
There are also those who do not grasp the meaning. One should reflect upon the essence of principle (*li*), which fundamentally lacks the four natures (*catur-nikāya*) and so forth;

thus, by dissolving emotion (*qing*) through principle, one attains this wondrous realization. As for the three thousand emotional phenomena (*qing-fa*) discussed in the *Four Treatises* (*Si-lun*), as previously argued, the three thousand are the virtues that are manifested.

Why then does the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* further correlate these with "non-dharmas" (*fei dao*)? It is said: if we speak within the context of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching (*yuan-dun jiao*), regarding dharmas...
The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*)—whether as phenomena (*vastu*) or principles (*tattva*), whether good or evil, pure or defiled—is such that there is no dharma to be abandoned.
That which is to be relinquished is merely the afflictions of the mind. Thus, the Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra states: "One should eliminate only the illness, not the dharma.

Once the illness has perished, the essence naturally returns to its original state. Furthermore, in various texts, "affliction" (*qing*) is also termed "phenomenon" (*shi*); thus, one takes the causal conditions from which they arise as the objective basis (*ālambana*).
To "shatter" [the inherent] is not yet understood. There are matters of the inherent principle (li-jù) and matters of emotional defilement (qíng-rǎn).

Within these, there is that which possesses both [inherence and defilement], and that which possesses one but not the other. Since matters of emotional defilement must be abandoned, it may also be said that the inherent principle is "shattered";

this is a dharma-gate. How could there be anything to abandon? If even abandonment is inadmissible, how much more so the talk of "shattering"? Yet, to regard the three thousand [realms] as non-Dharma—this is what is meant by "shattering."
This clearly demonstrates that the true and the deluded are non-dual, and that emotional afflictions do not depart from principle; therefore, it is presented in contrast to them.

It is just as the Four Ming [masters] used the cultivation of good and evil to correspond with the phenomenal creation—how could this possibly negate phenomenal creation? Thus, one should know that each passage has its own specific intent;
to speak of them in a general way would be to miss the point. Fifth is the section on the meaning of the Three Truths. Now, regarding the Three Thousand [realms] in relation to the Three Truths:

Regarding the presence or absence of marks (*lakṣaṇa*), the progression or regression of their meaning varies, and the phrasing further differs. For instance, if we speak in terms of "extinction" (*mṛga*) and "illumination" (*āloka*):

in extinction, the three truths (*trīṇi satyāni*) are all obliterated; if even emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and the provisional (*saṃvṛti*) cannot be apprehended, how much less can the three thousand [realms] (*tri-sahasra*)?

In illumination, even emptiness and the provisional are still merely provisional names (*prajñapti-nāma*); how much less can the three thousand? As it is said, "the three truths have no form," and again, "even within emptiness and the provisional..."
This is what is meant by "the peerless. Furthermore, since all three truths are provisionally established, what prevents us from discussing the three thousand realms in terms of emptiness?

This is because emptiness possesses the characteristic of pervasiveness. What prevents us from discussing the three thousand realms in terms of the provisional? This is because the provisional manifests the inherent completeness [of all phenomena]. What prevents us from discussing the three thousand realms in terms of the Middle Way? This is because the Middle Way is able to harmonize and encompass them all.
Nevertheless, when speaking in terms of the Middle and the extremes, although emptiness and the provisional possess the characteristics of pervasiveness and the body of completeness, respectively...
...its virtue is such that it harmoniously encompasses [all things]. The three thousand [realms] must, in turn, be understood as emptiness, the provisional, and the middle;
